[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot A" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116497 :tutorial/content "To compute the product of an elementary matrix and another matrix, one option is to perform the matrix multiplication as usual. However, there's an easier, quicker way.

Remember that every elementary matrix is the result of applying an elementary row operation to the identity matrix. If we multiply another matrix by an elementary matrix, we're effectively applying the elementary row operation to the other matrix.

For example, suppose we are asked to find the product $EA$ where
![](images/25/25d4c31649834fe3ae42a701d49f6e4a31fa8626de1d9aeed0f98ccbbf4a57fb.svg)

The elementary matrix $E$ comes from swapping the two rows of the identity matrix ($R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$). So, to compute the product $EA,$ all we have to do is swap the two rows of $A\mathbin{:}$
![](images/49/497b76accb211bbe4253ee2094206f70e8856f9510db71f6367f255fcc565665.svg)

This may seem almost too easy. But it's true! And we can verify it by computing the product the long way, using matrix multiplication. Indeed, we get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}EA & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 8 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we say that $E \cdot A$ is equivalent to applying to $A$ the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2.$

**Watch out!** It's important to multiply $A$ from the *left*. If we multiply $A$ by an elementary matrix from the *right*, we will perform a *column* operation on $A$ (not a row operation). In this case, multiplying $A$ by $E$ from the right will have the effect of switching the *columns* of $A,$ not the rows.

$$
\begin{aligned}AE & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 8 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 6 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133922 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" "question-688ce6d7-73b6-5ba5-87a1-28b0bc9bdadb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/id #uuid "01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/math-academy-id "q-161551" :question/problem "![](images/6e/6e5cb856069061be9b877753ce6c373ee9191547fce8750e9c2a8b073b99ceb0.png)

Given that $R$ is the type II region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V=$" :question/worked-solution "For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](images/e5/e5779dc92c875bef280425ed24a17cfb53f9f2a9736292a92ccdb988044237a6.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{y}^{2}.
$$

![](images/00/00f2847a8e4c927a1c6631f4aef03c57b9d28f18341b268182501ada07225382.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{y}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡z[x]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-25ad75a8-02de-5c76-b6ba-6c420483aaa3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Evaluate the triple integral

over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/b7/b7e71e46310b065e2c03b4a0aebaa96268136c7f633eea6983612297e56361d1.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/14/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}12x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1+y+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6(1+y+z)^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6z+6{y}^{2}z+2{z}^{3}+6y{z}^{2}+12yz+6{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+2+6y+12y+6)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+18y+14)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+18y+14)\,dy & =[2{y}^{3}+9{y}^{2}+14y]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(2+9+14)-0 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-52c6f404-4a46-5339-9b41-fcaeb9813680"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "4251c35b-5737-5f81-8168-9bb04b9bfceb" :question/math-academy-id "q-3894" :question/problem "Which of the following is a root of the polynomial ${v}^{4}-4{v}^{3}+7v-28?$

I. $v=-4$

II. $v=4$

III. $v=2$" :question/worked-solution "- Substituting $-4$ for $v$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)^{4}-4(-4)^{3}+7(-4)-28 & = \\ 256+256-28-28 & = \\ 456\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $-4$ is substituted for $v.$ Therefore, $-4$ is *not*  a root.

- Substituting $4$ for $v$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4)^{4}-4(4)^{3}+7(4)-28 & = \\ 256-256+28-28 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $4$ is substituted for $v.$ Therefore, $4$ is a root.

- Substituting $2$ for $v$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{4}-4(2)^{3}+7(2)-28 & = \\ 16-32+14-28 & = \\ -30\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $2$ is substituted for $v.$ Therefore, $2$ is *not*  a root.

Therefore, the root is $v=4,$ so the correct answer is "II only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-52ee438e-ac14-5d2d-9ba2-e23f74a8dc8e"] "Which of the following is a root of the polynomial ${u}^{4}-26{u}^{2}+25?$

I. $u=1$

II. $u=5$

III. $u=3$" :question/worked-solution "- Substituting $1$ for $u$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{4}-26(1)^{2}+25 & = \\ 1-26(1)+25 & = \\ 1-26+25 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $1$ is substituted for $u.$ Therefore, $1$ is a root.

- Substituting $5$ for $u$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5)^{4}-26(5)^{2}+25 & = \\ 625-26(25)+25 & = \\ 625-650+25 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $5$ is substituted for $u.$ Therefore, $5$ is a root.

- Substituting $3$ for $u$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3)^{4}-26(3)^{2}+25 & = \\ 81-26(9)+25 & = \\ 81-234+25 & = \\ -128\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $3$ is substituted for $u.$ Therefore, $3$ is *not*  a root.

Therefore, the roots are $u=1$ and $u=5,$ so the correct answer is "I and II only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields 17592186345055 :question/problem "Let $R=[1,3]\times [0,2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=x+y-1.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{1,2,3\},\,{P}_{2}=\{0,1,2\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the lower Riemann sum $L(f,P).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152149 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a55a479e-4a45-5971-8018-f156cd1ee741"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-a55a479e-4a45-5971-8018-f156cd1ee741" :question/id #uuid "a55a479e-4a45-5971-8018-f156cd1ee741" :question/math-academy-id "q-75252" :question/problem "Let $R=[0,4]\times [1,5]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=9-x-y.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{0,2,4\},\,{P}_{2}=\{1,3,5\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the lower Riemann sum $L(f,P).$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](images/97/97220aa0d23d01e807608e6194a37661ba77cc391d0adf537908c1f13b1b6de8.png)

The lower Riemann sum $L(f,P)$ is given by

$$
L(f,P)={m}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{m}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{m}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{m}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22})
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ is the minimum value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=4$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $L(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
L(f,P)=4{m}_{11}+4{m}_{21}+4{m}_{12}+4{m}_{22}.
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=9-x-y$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=9-x-y$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](images/30/306666a0e69fca9dc47c2295aa616a944482f00b28fdd96d9d96af816b058447.png)

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion.

![](images/15/15512c5f5063309474534a54b323d87c28cf9b776c10789a8f70e12cdb898aeb.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{11} & =f(2,3)=4 \\ {m}_{21} & =f(4,3)=2 \\ {m}_{12} & =f(2,5)=2 \\ {m}_{22} & =f(4,5)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
L(f,P)=4\cdot 4+4\cdot 2+4\cdot 2+4\cdot 0=32.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e7df747d-5ae6-580b-89b5-66c235ad174c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e7df747d-5ae6-580b-89b5-66c235ad174c" :answer-field/id #uuid "e7df747d-5ae6-580b-89b5-66c235ad174c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-258f88c7-c0a2-56e8-9230-059a60c0a8e3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ec56fda9-5a7a-576c-a3c2-f64506f5aa01" "answer-858f5818-4647-5518-b75d-f2e9dd90e7f8" "answer-258f88c7-c0a2-56e8-9230-059a60c0a8e3" "answer-b17bf7f2-0d3c-57ff-a579-7f0faaabe3b9" "answer-98578764-7601-57dc-9d67-e947a3ce724a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ec56fda9-5a7a-576c-a3c2-f64506f5aa01" :answer/id #uuid "ec56fda9-5a7a-576c-a3c2-f64506f5aa01" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-858f5818-4647-5518-b75d-f2e9dd90e7f8" :answer/id #uuid "858f5818-4647-5518-b75d-f2e9dd90e7f8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-258f88c7-c0a2-56e8-9230-059a60c0a8e3" :answer/id #uuid "258f88c7-c0a2-56e8-9230-059a60c0a8e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b17bf7f2-0d3c-57ff-a579-7f0faaabe3b9" :answer/id #uuid "b17bf7f2-0d3c-57ff-a579-7f0faaabe3b9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "36" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98578764-7601-57dc-9d67-e947a3ce724a" :answer/id #uuid "98578764-7601-57dc-9d67-e947a3ce724a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "40" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186345058 :question/problem "Let $R=[0,2]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=13-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.$

closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-x=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177843 :answer-field/correct 17592186177846 :answer-field/choices ["answer-b1c4f06f-dc17-5580-804b-5e960683c34d" "answer-6d43715d-8bf7-5ec2-8e40-279a007829e7" "answer-d72ed648-66b7-5576-93c4-769d0caa8136" "answer-090f3e9e-10f1-5380-9922-651ecfe6ea3a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1c4f06f-dc17-5580-804b-5e960683c34d" :answer/id #uuid "b1c4f06f-dc17-5580-804b-5e960683c34d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-10\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d43715d-8bf7-5ec2-8e40-279a007829e7" :answer/id #uuid "6d43715d-8bf7-5ec2-8e40-279a007829e7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-5\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d72ed648-66b7-5576-93c4-769d0caa8136" :answer/id #uuid "d72ed648-66b7-5576-93c4-769d0caa8136" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-090f3e9e-10f1-5380-9922-651ecfe6ea3a" :answer/id #uuid "090f3e9e-10f1-5380-9922-651ecfe6ea3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b2316759-1f4d-59b3-aebb-24c5b1ac8267" :question/id #uuid "b2316759-1f4d-59b3-aebb-24c5b1ac8267" :question/math-academy-id "q-127061" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i-xy\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-xy=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt=du,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}6{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0fe3669d-5fb8-5cf8-8402-eaff7b7d0308"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $F(x,y)=xi+\frac{1}{4}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(\frac{1}{4})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+16t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0+32\pi -1)-(0-1) \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b1fc0cd0-57f3-5df9-9d82-31c607584763"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-4696ec15-27d3-55f9-a25e-60bb43e6e055" :question/id #uuid "4696ec15-27d3-55f9-a25e-60bb43e6e055" :question/math-academy-id "q-127075" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+(2+x)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}=8{sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2+x=2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}16{u}^{3}+16u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d2ae6c02-1c78-5b5d-926b-2d33957e08c9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-576a1cb3-98a9-5ffe-af11-d33bc3dd7a74"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133550 :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $a_n = 8 \cdot 3^n$ for $n\geq 1.$  What is the recursive formula for this sequence?" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_n.
$$

To complete the formula,  we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1.$ The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =8\cdot {3}^{1}=8\cdot 3=24, \\ {a}_{2} & =8\cdot {3}^{2}=8\cdot 9=72.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{72}{24}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric  sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = 3 a_n, \quad a_1 = 24, \quad n \geq 1.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133933 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c9893d5c-f0eb-5a20-a7b0-6d7123b5cbef" "question-cfd63bcb-672d-5a91-b2cf-d24e8a457ef0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133536 :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $f(n) =\dfrac{6}{(-2)^n}$ for $n\geq 1.$  What is the recursive formula for this sequence?" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = r \cdot f(n).
$$

To complete the formula, we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1.$ The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =\frac{6}{(-2)^{1}}=\frac{6}{(-2)}=-3, \\ f(2) & =\frac{6}{(-2)^{2}}=\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{f(2)}{f(1)}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{(-3)}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = -\dfrac{1}{2} f(n), \qquad f(1) = -3, \qquad n \geq 1.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133934 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9a2f8eb3-e0d7-5d85-8fb5-62ab15cba80d" "question-98925317-9d30-5e69-bd45-e05c5755cffe"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133537 :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence

$$
a_{n+1} = 3a_n,\, \qquad a_1 = 1,\, \qquad n\geq 1?
$$" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}, \qquad n \geq 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term $a_1$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1=1.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_n
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r = 3.$

Substituting $a_1 = 1$ and $r = 3$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}	\[5pt]
&= 1 \cdot 3^{n-1} \[5pt]
&= 3^{n-1}.
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=3^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133935 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5e4e0f75-9894-567b-a1a8-c012ad934066" "question-a040fd0d-33b9-5cd2-ba84-4a64f3c5606d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133551 :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the sequence

$$
f(n+1) =-\dfrac{f(n)}{3},\, \quad f(1) = {\color{blue}9},\, \quad n\geq 1?
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite our recursive formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n+1)=-\frac{f(n)}{3}=-\frac{1}{3}f(n)\end{aligned}
$$

The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n) =f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $f(1)=9.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
f(n+1) = {\color{red}r} \cdot f(n)
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r = -\dfrac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $f(1) = 9$ and $r = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
f(n) &= f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}	\[5pt]
&= 9 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}.
}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =9\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n-1} \\  & =9\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{-1}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n} \\  & =9\cdot (-\frac{3}{1})\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n} \\  & =-27\cdot \frac{1}{(-3)^{n}} \\  & =-\frac{27}{(-3)^{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=-\dfrac{27}{(-3)^n} ,\quad n\geq 1.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-1246524a-95f9-5d04-bcaf-769f77cf931a" :question/id #uuid "1246524a-95f9-5d04-bcaf-769f77cf931a" :question/math-academy-id "q-251874" :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is ${a}_{n}=5\cdot {4}^{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ What is the recursive formula for this sequence? Express your answer in terms of ${a}_{n}.$

${a}_{n+1}=$
{{field-1}}$,\,{a}_{1}=$
{{field-2}}$,\,n\ge 1$" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}.
$$

To complete the formula, we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term ${a}_{1}.$ The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =5\cdot {4}^{1}=5\cdot 4=20, \\ {a}_{2} & =5\cdot {4}^{2}=5\cdot 16=80.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{80}{20}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric sequence is

Substituting ${a}_{1}=-\frac{4}{5}$ and $r=\frac{1}{4}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}

the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence given by

$$
f(n+1)=\frac{f(n)}{6},\,\,f(1)=4,\,\,n\ge 1?
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite our recursive formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n+1)=\frac{f(n)}{6}=\frac{1}{6}f(n)\end{aligned}
$$

The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n)=f(1)\cdot {r}^{n-1},\,n\ge 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $f(1)=4.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
f(n+1)=r\cdot f(n)
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r=\frac{1}{6}.$

Substituting $f(1)=4$ and $r=\frac{1}{6}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =4\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n-1} \\  & =4\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{-1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{6}{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n} \\  & =24\cdot \frac{1}{{6}^{n}} \\  & =\frac{24}{{6}^{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=\frac{24}{{6}^{n}},\,n\ge 1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6d6b8a21-70e2-5b57-a0a2-6cb7c4f3a1b7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6d6b8a21-70e2-5b57-a0a2-6cb7c4f3a1b7" :answer-field/id #uuid "6d6b8a21-70e2-5b57-a0a2-6cb7c4f3a1b7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e877ea80-a0f4-50cc-b19e-fc100855d57b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e877ea80-a0f4-50cc-b19e-fc100855d57b" "answer-cc85700b-91d3-5f37-a0fd-d0b78d1f06ad" "answer-4c48d543-2d3c-51bb-a7bf-0270b3661c4a" "answer-e5c2c41c-0f75-5fa4-a688-22bb4ee3f293" "answer-9b8329a8-9240-5aad-b604-d9ff98436aa2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e877ea80-a0f4-50cc-b19e-fc100855d57b" :answer/id #uuid "e877ea80-a0f4-50cc-b19e-fc100855d57b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(n)=\frac{24}{{6}^{n}},\,n\ge 1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cc85700b-91d3-5f37-a0fd-d0b78d1f06ad" :answer/id #uuid "cc85700b-91d3-5f37-a0fd-d0b78d1f06ad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(n)=\frac{2}{{24}^{n}},\,n\ge 1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c48d543-2d3c-51bb-a7bf-0270b3661c4a" :answer/id #uuid "4c48d543-2d3c-51bb-a7bf-0270b3661c4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(n)=\frac{2}{{6}^{n}},\,n\ge 1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e5c2c41c-0f75-5fa4-a688-22bb4ee3f293" :answer/id #uuid "e5c2c41c-0f75-5fa4-a688-22bb4ee3f293" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(n)=\frac{4}{{6}^{n}},\,n\ge 1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9b8329a8-9240-5aad-b604-d9ff98436aa2" :answer/id #uuid "9b8329a8-9240-5aad-b604-d9ff98436aa2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(n)={24}^{n},\,n\ge 1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135016 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the following **explicit formula** for a geometric sequence:

$$
a_n = 2\cdot 5^{n-1}, \qquad n\geq 1
$$

We can write this geometric sequence using a recursive formula. Recall that the recursive formula for *any* geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r\cdot a_n.
$$

To convert from the explicit formula to the recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common ratio. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2\cdot {5}^{0}=2\cdot 1=2 \\ {a}_{2} & =2\cdot {5}^{1}=2\cdot 5=10,\end{aligned}
$$

and the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{10}{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}2}$ and the common ratio is $r={\color{red}5}.$ Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}5} \cdot a_n, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}2}, \qquad n \geq 1
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135017 :tutorial/content "It's often more useful to translate from the recursive formula to an explicit one. So how do we find the explicit formula for the geometric sequence defined recursively as

$$
a_{n+1} ={\color{red}\dfrac 1 4} a_n,\, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}2},\, \qquad n\geq 1?
$$

The explicit formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1,
$$

so we just need to determine the first term $a_1$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}2}.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n+1} & =r\cdot {a}_{n} \\ {a}_{n+1} & =\frac{1}{4}{a}_{n}\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, we see that ${\color{red}r} = {\color{red}\dfrac 1 4}.$

Now we substitute $a_1={\color{blue}2}$ and $r={\color{red}\dfrac{1}{4}}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\eqalign{
a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \
&= {\color{blue}2} \cdot \left( {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{4}} \right)^{n-1}		
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=2 \cdot \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134050 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166936 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174" :question/id #uuid "77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174" :question/math-academy-id "q-336705" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into $\text{L1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields Given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{7}{3},$ calculate the area (in square units) of $△ABC$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{7}{3}.$ Notice that relative to $∠A,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{BC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AC} \\ \frac{7}{3} & =\frac{4x-1}{x+1} \\ 7(x+1) & =3(4x-1) \\ 7x+7 & =12x-3 \\ 7x-12x & =-3-7 \\ -5x & =-10 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =x+1=2+1=3, \\ BC & =4x-1=4(2)-1=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 7 \\  & =10.5.\end{aligned}

Given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{9}{8},$ calculate the area (in square units) of $△ABC$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{9}{8}.$ Notice that relative to $∠A,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{BC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AC} \\ \frac{9}{8} & =\frac{4x-2}{3x+1} \\ 9(3x+1) & =8(4x-2) \\ 27x+9 & =32x-16 \\ 9+16 & =32x-27x \\ 25 & =5x \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =4x-2=4(5)-2=18, \\ AC & =3x+1=3(5)+1=16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 16\cdot 18 \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aab0fb0a-8165-54b3-b1b3-36d377c7585d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id We are given that $m∠B={35}^{∘}.$ Notice that relative to $∠B,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{AC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{BC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠B) & =\frac{AC}{BC} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘}) & =\frac{x+2}{2x} \\ 2x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘}) & =x+2 \\ 2x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘})-x & =2 \\ x(2\operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘})-1) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{2\operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘})-1} \\ x & =4.994\,8…\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}BC & =2x=2(4.994\,8…)=9.989\,6…, \\ AC & =x+2=(4.994\,8…)+2=6.994\,8….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$

"question-be91f77e-a6ef-5326-b655-78aac371668c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175850 :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:
![](images/a7/a7c708ba41cf7369d6d99e43389c1a4d52e92c77d7051ced888fd57c111c82a9.svg)
If $Y = |X|,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the transformation $Y = |X|$ is two-to-one over the interval $-3\lt x \lt 3.$ 

![](images/8b/8bc657a6b1b0defb0857f665ae48353862f06e0145bbc22ad3dac906da720380.png)

Moreover, for $-3\lt x \lt 3,$ we have that $0 \leq y \lt 3.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \leq      y <           3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(|X|\le y) \\  & =P(-y\le X\le y) \\  & ={F}_{X}(y)-{F}_{X}(-y).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \leq      y <           3,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & ={F}_{X}^{′}(y)-(-1){F}_{X}^{′}(-y) \\  & ={F}_{X}^{′}(y)+{F}_{X}^{′}(-y) \\  & ={f}_{X}(y)+{f}_{X}(-y).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={f}_{X}(y)+{f}_{X}(-y) \\  & =\frac{1}{24}(y+1)^{2}+\frac{1}{24}(-y+1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}[({y}^{2}+2y+1)+({y}^{2}-2y+1)] \\  & =\frac{1}{24}(2{y}^{2}+2) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}({y}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

![](images/73/732a2d8d53f1424b086596203b917e51f1e791bdaef7b638eb109f3ee5600219.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176073 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1a1ee509-91e0-56a1-9d72-7806568cd6ce" "question-97ae858a-243f-5feb-afeb-22f3b7dc533e" "question-a04f88da-8653-5b9a-90b7-8404ed30a5a3" "question-f55a1e43-e983-59db-880e-46aa1036ba76" "question-858574ee-13d7-5994-a0b6-afd2faa00bae"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175690 :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:
![](images/5e/5e5fdd7655bb0cb4858b2a723f3eb3a7bf16c290b98dde097153c0bc78c4ac54.svg)
If the probability density function of $Y = X^2$ is given by 
![](images/d4/d436eaaafafcc03b81ac40cd746dcdf7728055cab8ea6c3ac1f3cb36279fd219.svg)
find the function $h(y).$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's visualize the transformation $Y = X^2$ over the interval $-1 <            x <         2.$

![](images/c9/c98b2d947486e4666380dc8412c1b64a8518c84e39372052602a9402ab3d4211.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $-1 \lt   x <       1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \lt  y \lt 1.$

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $1 \leq x \lt  2.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $1 \leq  y \lt   4.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $1 \leq  y \lt   4.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $1 \leq  y \lt   4,$ we have

$$

$$

Notice that we used $|X| = X$ for $X > 0.$

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $1 \leq  y \lt   4,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{5}{33}(\sqrt{y})^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{5}{33}{y}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{66}\,{y}^{3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $1\le y<5,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})].\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$

If $Y={(1-X)}^{2},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the transformation $Y={(1-X)}^{2}$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-1<x<3.$

Moreover, for $-1<x<3,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $0\le y<4.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0\le y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({(1-X)}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}\le 1-X\le {y}^{1/2}) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}-1\le -X\le {y}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =P(1-{y}^{1/2}\le X\le 1+{y}^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0\le y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{1+{y}^{1/2}}{4}+\frac{1-{y}^{1/2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}, & 0\le y<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c8b4d77c-02ba-56ca-a4f9-ffe483ffd99e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "1a1ee509-91e0-56a1-9d72-7806568cd6ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-144920" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{12}(2-x), & -3<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y={X}^{2}$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<1 \\ h(y), & 1\le y<9 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $g(y).$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's visualize the transformation $Y={X}^{2}$ over the interval $-3<x<1.$

![](images/73/7332c58097d1a2933c10152028bc715a147e820ae14b2fae92fe288eaf956ce0.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $-3<x\le -1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $1\le y<9.$

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $-1<x<1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<1.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<1.$ 

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt{y}\le X\le \sqrt{y}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(\sqrt{y})-{F}_{X}(-\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(-\sqrt{y})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(-\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}(\frac{1}{12}(2-\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{12}(2+\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{1}{6\sqrt{y}}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1dd61ae8-a6f5-545b-bade-944272de3e4b"] :db/ensure find the function $h(y).$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ over the interval $0<x<4.$

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $2\le x<4.$ On this interval,  $Y$ is nonzero on  $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2}.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2}.$ 

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(\frac{1}{2}|X-1|\le y) \\  & =P(|X-1|\le 2y) \\  & =P(X-1\le 2y) \\  & =P(X\le 2y+1) \\  & ={F}_{X}(2y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used $|X-1|=X-1$ for $X>1.$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2},$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =2{F}_{X}^{′}(2y+1) \\  & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{8}(2y+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2y+1).\end{aligned}

"Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2-x}, & x\ge 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y=(X-4)^{2}$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<4 \\ h(y), & y\ge 4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $g(y).$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=(X-4)^{2}$ over the interval $x\ge 2.$

![](images/77/77008820197d69dc81d674a48e207b7527d2f3d4cc1d0ca3ed8ad4d8553665b8.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $2<x<6.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<4.$

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $x\ge 6.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $y\ge 4.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<4.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P((X-4)^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt{y}\le X-4\le \sqrt{y}) \\  & =P(4-\sqrt{y}\le X\le 4+\sqrt{y}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})-{F}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(4+\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(4-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({e}^{2-4-\sqrt{y}}+{e}^{2-4+\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{y}-2}+{e}^{\sqrt{y}-2}}{2\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{y}-2}+{e}^{\sqrt{y}-2}}{2\sqrt{y}}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $$

where $u(X)$ is a function of $X.$

We can use the distribution function method to compute the PDF of $Y.$ Broadly speaking, the distribution function method involves the following two steps:

- Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y$ of $Y.$

We've already seen how we use the distribution function technique to find the PDF of $Y$ in cases where $u(X)$ is strictly monotonic (i.e., strictly increasing or decreasing). If $u(X)$ is monotonic, then there is a one-to-one correspondence between $Y$ and $X,$ so computing the PDF of $Y$ is reasonably straightforward.

We can also use the distribution function method in cases where $u$ is not monotonic, although a little more care is needed. This is what we'll focus on in this lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177062 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$

Moreover, for $0 < |x| < 2,$ we have that $-1 \lt y \lt 3.$ 

Let's use the distribution function method to calculate the probability density function of $Y.$

Consider the interval $-1 < y < 3.$ We write down the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ and then use our transformation to isolate $X$ in the parentheses. This will allow us to write $F_Y$ in terms of $F_X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}-1\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}\le y+1) \\  & =P(-(y+1)^{1/2}\le X\le (y+1)^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}((y+1)^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(-(y+1)^{1/2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $-1 \lt      y <          3,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule, as usual. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y+1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}((y+1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y+1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-(y+1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y+1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}((y+1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y+1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-(y+1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y+1)^{-1/2}({f}_{X}((y+1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y+1)^{1/2})).\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

![](images/c7/c72cad36ae780f6de29b485e8636244b8ca7889de06ca287dccc0569b933c84a.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177059 :tutorial/content "We know how to compute the PDF of $Y = u(X)$ in cases where $u$ is either one-to-one or two-to-one over the entire support of $X.$ Let's now expand this to cases where $u(X)$ is both one-to-one and many-to-one over different intervals.

$$

$$

$$

$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $-\frac{3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}y & =2 \\ (-\frac{3}{2})\cdot (-\frac{2}{3}y) & =(-\frac{3}{2})\cdot (2) \\ (\cancel{-\frac{3}{2}})\cdot (\cancel{-\frac{2}{3}}y) & =-\frac{6}{2} \\ y & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|3-\frac{2}{3}y|=-(3-\frac{2}{3}y),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|3-\frac{2}{3}y| & =5 \\ -(3-\frac{2}{3}y) & =5 \\ -3+\frac{2}{3}y & =5 \\ \frac{2}{3}y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $\frac{3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}y & =8 \\ (\frac{3}{2})\cdot (\frac{2}{3}y) & =(\frac{3}{2})\cdot (8) \\ (\cancel{\frac{3}{2}})\cdot (\cancel{\frac{2}{3}}y) & =\frac{24}{2} \\ y & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|5y-1| & =6 \\ 5y-1 & =6 \\ 5y & =7 \\ \frac{5y}{5} & =\frac{7}{5} \\ y & =\frac{7}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|5y-1|=-(5y-1),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5y-1| & =6 \\ -(5y-1) & =6 \\ -5y+1 & =6 \\ -5y & =5 \\ \frac{-5y}{-5} & =\frac{5}{-5} \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

"Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{3}{4},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)=\frac{a\sqrt{2}-b\sqrt{14}}{8},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$"] ["question-43bdc32f-8f5e-5fac-84f7-776394b1cc9e" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v,$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{2}{4} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})+(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{14}}{8}+\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}-1\sqrt{14}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=3,b=1,$ and $a+b=4.$"] ["question-43bdc32f-8f5e-5fac-84f7-776394b1cc9e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-afbfba15-89cd-5f8b-8d11-e527ad3d57cb" $$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v,$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive, we take

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{24}{25})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})+(\frac{7}{25})(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{24\sqrt{3}}{50}+\frac{7}{50} \\  & =\frac{24\sqrt{3}+7}{50}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1059df0b-e279-5183-9a0b-f6c9c0f186a7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3710dd2a-0992-5c4b-b6c5-20c3ea7c9d8f" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{5}{13})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{5}^{2}}{{13}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{25}{169} \\  & =\frac{169}{169}-\frac{25}{169} \\  & =\frac{144}{169}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{144}{169}} \\  & =\pm \frac{12}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=-\frac{12}{13}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{12}{13})(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(\frac{5}{13})(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{12\sqrt{2}}{26}-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{26} \\  & =-\frac{17\sqrt{2}}{26}\end{aligned}

"question-77e70b3f-8704-511e-87c9-d67cfcbe9ec9"] [17592186185350 :tutorial/content "We can compute trigonometric ratios using the sum and difference formulas for cosine together with the Pythagorean identity.

Let's suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\sin u = \dfrac{1}{3}, \qquad
\sin v = \dfrac {3}{5}, \qquad
\cos v = -\dfrac{4}{5}.
$$

How can we find the value of $\cos\left(u - v\right)$ given that $u$ lies in the second quadrant?

First, we recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\cos(u - v) = \cos u \cos v + \sin u \sin v
$$

We know the values of $\sin{u}$, $\sin{v}$, and $\cos{v}.$ To find the missing value of $\cos{u}$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 u + \cos^2 u = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \cos^2 u = 1- \sin^2 u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9}-\frac{1}{9} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{8}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have

$$
\cos u= -\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula:

$$
\eqalign{
		\cos(u - v) 
			&= \cos u \cos v + \sin u \sin v \[5pt]
			&= \left( -\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \right) \left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right) +  \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) \[5pt]			
 			&= \dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{15} + \dfrac{3}{15} \[5pt]
			&= \dfrac{8\sqrt{2}+3}{15}
	}
$$"] [17592186184424 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0] ["question-e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a" :question/id #uuid "e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a"] ["question-e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a" :question/math-academy-id "q-97869"] ["question-e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a" :question/problem "A matrix $B$ has the characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda =0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\lambda =2$ is a root of the characteristic equation

II. $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $B$

III. $B$ is non-invertible"] ["question-e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a" :question/worked-solution "The invertible matrix theorem in terms of eigenvectors states the following:

*The square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A.$*

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, substituting $\lambda =2$ into the equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda  & =0 \\ (2)^{3}+2(2)^{2}-2 & =0 \\ 8+8-2 & =0 \\ 14 & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $\lambda =0$ is a root of the characteristic equation. As a result, $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $B.$

- Statement III is true. Since $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $B,$ according to the invertible matrix theorem, $B$ is non-invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-e7077a60-6a06-585e-8213-5137d377235a"] [17592186125071 :question/problem "If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ invertible matrix, then which of the following could be the characteristic equation of With that in mind, let's examine the given equations in turn.

- Equation I **cannot** be the characteristic equation of $A$ since $\lambda =0$ is a root of the equation.

- Equation II could be the characteristic equation of $A.$ Indeed, $\lambda =0$ is not a root of the equation.

- Equation III **cannot** be the characteristic equation of $A$ since $\lambda =0$ is a root of the equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""] [17592186125071 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186123026 :answer-field/correct 17592186123031] ["question-a1882648-2096-59b1-b0c6-167402b1eeb7" :question/id #uuid "a1882648-2096-59b1-b0c6-167402b1eeb7"] ["question-a1882648-2096-59b1-b0c6-167402b1eeb7" :question/math-academy-id "q-97895"] ["question-a1882648-2096-59b1-b0c6-167402b1eeb7" :question/problem "If $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\lambda =1$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $(A-I)x=0$ has a nonzero solution

II. $\text{Col}(A-I)={R}^{3}$

III. $\text{nullity}(A-I)\ne 0$"] ["question-a1882648-2096-59b1-b0c6-167402b1eeb7" :question/worked-solution "Given a $3\times 3$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=3=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Let's now apply the theorem to the matrix $M=A-I.$

- Statement I is true. Notice that if $\lambda =1$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ then the nonzero solutions of $(A-I)x=0$ are eigenvectors of $A.$ As a result, the matrix $M=A-I$ must be singular.

- Statement II is false. Since $M=A-I$ is singular, by the invertible matrix theorem, we obtain that

$$
\text{Col}(A-I)\ne {R}^{3}.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $M=A-I$ is singular, by the invertible matrix theorem, we obtain that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-I)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-a1882648-2096-59b1-b0c6-167402b1eeb7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] {{field-1}}"] ["question-51d9f041-304f-5c22-9ed6-3b3659033e6d" :question/worked-solution "According to the sum and constant multiple rules, we can compute the required limit as follows:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}(5f(x)+6g(x)+3{x}^{3})=5{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)+6{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)+3{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}{x}^{3}
$$

 

The above equation assumes that ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)$ both exist.

From the graph, we see ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)=0,$ and from part 3, we found ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)=1.$ So, we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}(5f(x)+6g(x)+3{x}^{3}) & =5{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)+6{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)+3{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}{x}^{3} \\  & =5\cdot 0+6\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)^{3} \\  & =0+6-3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-51d9f041-304f-5c22-9ed6-3b3659033e6d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c" :answer-field/id #uuid "0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c"] ["answer-65d21ca8-3efe-54e5-bade-78de16222794" :answer/id #uuid "65d21ca8-3efe-54e5-bade-78de16222794"] ["answer-65d21ca8-3efe-54e5-bade-78de16222794" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-65d21ca8-3efe-54e5-bade-78de16222794" :answer/value "3"] ["answer-field-0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c" :answer-field/correct "answer-65d21ca8-3efe-54e5-bade-78de16222794"] ["answer-field-0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c" :answer-field/choices "answer-65d21ca8-3efe-54e5-bade-78de16222794"] ["question-51d9f041-304f-5c22-9ed6-3b3659033e6d" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-0f20ff5c-92ae-5166-a3cb-7910d80b3b2c"] [17592186124613 :knowledge-point/questions "question-51d9f041-304f-5c22-9ed6-3b3659033e6d"] ["question-7b122753-4256-5b6b-bc1d-003f930bcebd" :question/id #uuid "7b122753-4256-5b6b-bc1d-003f930bcebd"] ["question-7b122753-4256-5b6b-bc1d-003f930bcebd" :question/math-academy-id "q-131467"] ["question-7b122753-4256-5b6b-bc1d-003f930bcebd" :question/problem "What are the points of discontinuity of $f(x)?$

linear regression in two variables, say $x$ and $y,$ our task is to find a straight line that best fits a set of data points $(x_i,y_i).$ We can easily extend this technique to situations involving three variables. 

The following table shows the number of units $x_1$ and $x_2$ (in hundreds) of two goods produced by a small company in several production runs and the respective profits $y$ (in thousands of dollars) obtained by the company.   

| Good Type 1 $(x_1)$ | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Good Type 2 $(x_2)$ | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$6$** |
| Profit $(y)$ | $6$ | $15$ | $18$ | $24$ |

Since we now have three variables, $x_1, x_2,$ and $y,$ our task is to find a *plane* of the form

$$
y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
$$

that best fits the data.

![](images/ce/ced34ebf098fd20194fafd74f4f75bf855707ad1457e706264c9e922a7efa706.png)

  

Substituting the values of $x_1$ and $x_2$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}+2{\beta }_{2}=6 \\ {\beta }_{0}+2{\beta }_{1}+3{\beta }_{2}=15 \\ {\beta }_{0}+3{\beta }_{1}+4{\beta }_{2}=18 \\ {\beta }_{0}+4{\beta }_{1}+6{\beta }_{2}=24\end{aligned}
$$

This system can be expressed in matrix notation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 15 \\ 18 \\ 24\end{aligned}]}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

As usual, $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the coefficient vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector. 

Since our points do not all lie on a plane, there will be no parameters $\beta_0,$ $\beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0,$ $\beta_1,$ and $\beta_2$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the plane that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the plane of best fit (regression plane) is 

$$
y = 2+ 7x_1-x_2.
$$

    

Note that we can use the same technique to fit data involving more variables. For example, if we have four variables $x_1, x_2, x_3,$ and $y,$ then we can find a four-dimensional **hyperplane** of the form

$$
y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3
$$

that best fits a set of data points $(x_{1i},x_{2i}, x_{3i}, y).$  The coefficients of this hyperplane are found by solving the corresponding least-squares problem. 

Finally, applying linear regression to situations involving three or more variables is called **multiple linear regression**."] [17592186135145 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might need to place a constraint on the regression plane that forces it to pass through the origin.

$$

where $C$ is a constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =\frac{C}{1+1} \\ 6 & =\frac{C}{2} \\ C & =12\end{aligned}

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\},\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -15\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-226b9b94-926b-577f-834a-35ff659d1159" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$, where ${x}_{i}=\frac{x\cdot {q}_{i}}{{q}_{i}\cdot {q}_{i}}.$ Computing ${x}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{x\cdot {q}_{2}}{{q}_{2}\cdot {q}_{2}} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 4+(-15)\cdot 3}{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{40-45}{25} \\  & =\frac{-5}{25} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
15{x}_{2}=15\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=-3.
$$"] ["question-226b9b94-926b-577f-834a-35ff659d1159" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3231d9e1-5db0-532b-9d06-68eafedeb402" :answer-field/id #uuid "step-0d255e3d-83de-58fa-a2fb-4134cf57d2f5"] [17592186167196 :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186167196 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-4a051744-2fdf-5555-a542-727518fba033" :answer/id #uuid "4a051744-2fdf-5555-a542-727518fba033"] ["question-9669b6bb-a27d-584f-935a-b35adacb11c6" :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$"] ["question-9669b6bb-a27d-584f-935a-b35adacb11c6" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 12\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 8 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}52 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9669b6bb-a27d-584f-935a-b35adacb11c6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6730a75f-f272-5493-a8bf-085f7b4def46" :answer-field/id #uuid Let $y=\frac{1}{2}Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b)=\frac{1}{2}A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}A)}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{1}{2}A)}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & ={A}^{T}(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{T}(\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}16 \\ 34\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}8 \\ 17\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}62 \\ 45\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-2 \\ 2-2 \\ 2-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186208956 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-5c297385-0d1a-5107-874a-c1a917db787a" :answer/id #uuid "5c297385-0d1a-5107-874a-c1a917db787a"] ["answer-5c297385-0d1a-5107-874a-c1a917db787a" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-5c297385-0d1a-5107-874a-c1a917db787a" :answer/value "0"] [17592186205483 :answer-field/correct "answer-5c297385-0d1a-5107-874a-c1a917db787a"] [17592186205483 :answer-field/choices "answer-5c297385-0d1a-5107-874a-c1a917db787a"] ["answer-e894abe3-5313-5592-b411-4e2a239ad1f5" :answer/id #uuid "e894abe3-5313-5592-b411-4e2a239ad1f5"] ["answer-e894abe3-5313-5592-b411-4e2a239ad1f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-e894abe3-5313-5592-b411-4e2a239ad1f5" :answer/value "0"] [17592186205484 :answer-field/correct "answer-e894abe3-5313-5592-b411-4e2a239ad1f5"] [17592186205484 :answer-field/choices "answer-e894abe3-5313-5592-b411-4e2a239ad1f5"] ["answer-98db11c5-6460-500c-9ec8-23a74a1cf7f1" :answer/id #uuid "98db11c5-6460-500c-9ec8-23a74a1cf7f1"] ["answer-98db11c5-6460-500c-9ec8-23a74a1cf7f1" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-98db11c5-6460-500c-9ec8-23a74a1cf7f1" :answer/value "-4"] [17592186205482 :answer-field/correct "answer-98db11c5-6460-500c-9ec8-23a74a1cf7f1"] [17592186205482 :answer-field/choices "answer-98db11c5-6460-500c-9ec8-23a74a1cf7f1"] ["question-a5918743-e3c0-5f81-afbc-29edc571e474" :question/id #uuid "a5918743-e3c0-5f81-afbc-29edc571e474"] ["question-a5918743-e3c0-5f81-afbc-29edc571e474" :question/math-academy-id "q-276048"] ["question-a5918743-e3c0-5f81-afbc-29edc571e474" :question/problem "Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by

$$

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -4 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4+0-3 \\ -3+0+2 \\ -3+0+4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a5918743-e3c0-5f81-afbc-29edc571e474" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2bf6b302-f637-57b2-adae-46550fb30727" :answer-field/id #uuid
