</tbody></table>"] ["question-c1ab528e-b16d-505b-916d-2fee71d7c43b" :question/worked-solution "Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+0+0 \\ 0+0+0 \\ 1+0+0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c1ab528e-b16d-505b-916d-2fee71d7c43b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-569e10d0-4a91-5fcf-b1cd-04a5cc9a1035" :answer-field/id #uuid First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $2{y}_{1}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the given curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2} & =6 \\ {y}_{1}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

the quadratic form $Q(x)=5{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=52
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=13\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-13.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=13,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-13I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5\end{aligned}]-13[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 12 \\ 12 & -18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-13,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-13)I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5\end{aligned}]+13[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}18 & 12 \\ 12 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-e1eb45be-51da-5fe4-b582-bc025ec9533a" $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-8{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=9
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=8\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-9.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-8I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-9)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}]+9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A+9I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-0f7fea28-dc13-51b3-b3d3-9108cf056cc8" $$
A=[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=15
$$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=15\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=5.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

$$
\begin{aligned}A-15I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-15[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

"question-71a50d5a-430c-5d52-842d-aa1bb8a09b41"] [17592186163231 :tutorial/content "Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables 

$$
\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}
$$

that transforms the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ into the quadratic form $\mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. 

The columns of the matrix $P$ are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of $A,$ which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the **principal axes** of the quadratic form.

Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation 

$$
6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,
$$

and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

![](images/d8/d8a6b6dff52e0c4004432f9447b5fd484612eaacf07588c3469af143b0a9e880.png)

It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,
$$

which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

So, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}$

![](images/2a/2a4229ed50ef304e06cec6a64a3fa522a0aa679b70ebc1608b9042aedbbed2ef.svg)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +14 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/85/85e44a8dc5afeda8a266dca013f4298e7e475ea6ce7808cfe3072b4b23186334.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 
![](images/81/81c9b8b9f946e7c427bae2c1a7efa0a57c9f0388c9d67d846a14971bf9f33902.svg)

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/d6/d62eeed8be7829fc1d145697fb700d5f282ceaf45c3d967a8cb1270b4399f906.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 
![](images/61/6123f9b7e7cce970066dea2ab36a4e1d2704a17af961d03e016d83683eb13124.svg)

Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

$\qquad$ ![](images/f1/f10b4edf9545e958d4f32a695da26077c1ab7baf096c0956f1e02ba9ec94c8bd.svg) and ![](images/04/04a614acc9a6be123cdd1a8c765853a822da12f07137baaefef9f4715c59a5f3.svg)

Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes $y_1$ and $y_2.$ 

![](images/10/10a2f0ccd179eba7f65410f932548d954a459e1bc8dcb0803a5b2d9fe7896432.png)

In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to 

$$
7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.
$$

 

Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2} & =14 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{7}.$"] [17592186162224 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0] ["question-caaab3b2-6a76-5915-aacc-0fc605ea0da3" :question/id #uuid "caaab3b2-6a76-5915-aacc-0fc605ea0da3"] ["question-caaab3b2-6a76-5915-aacc-0fc605ea0da3" :question/math-academy-id "q-143052"] ["question-caaab3b2-6a76-5915-aacc-0fc605ea0da3" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=(x-1)^{2}-1$ for $x\le 1.$"] ["question-caaab3b2-6a76-5915-aacc-0fc605ea0da3" :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=(x-1)^{2}-1
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y:$

$$
x=(y-1)^{2}-1
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(y-1)^{2}-1 \\ x+1 & =(y-1)^{2} \\ -\sqrt{x+1} & =y-1 \\ 1-\sqrt{x+1} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we take the negative square root because if $x\le 1$ is the domain of $f,$ then the range of the inverse is ${f}^{-1}\le 1.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x):$

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=1-\sqrt{x+1}
$$"] ["question-caaab3b2-6a76-5915-aacc-0fc605ea0da3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-819f5105-b28d-5bf8-9cd7-60f7aa0b0ec1" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

    

To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=-(x-2)^{2}+4
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y:$

$$
x=-(y-2)^{2}+4
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-(y-2)^{2}+4 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4-x \\ y-2 & =-\sqrt{4-x} \\ y & =2-\sqrt{4-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we selected the negative square root because if the domain of $f(x)$ is $x\le 2,$ then the range of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ is  ${f}^{-1}\le 2.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x):$

$$

$$"] ["question-b20bccf7-d7c5-5c00-be58-d20d6291b56b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ed9666c1-5e34-582c-9b93-504bb7cbd0c8" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{2}-6x+11 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})-{3}^{2}+11 \\  & =(x-3)^{2}-9+11 \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

    

To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y=(x-3)^{2}+2
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y$:

$$
x=(y-3)^{2}+2
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(y-3)^{2}+2 \\ x-2 & =(y-3)^{2} \\ \sqrt{x-2} & =y-3 \\ \sqrt{x-2}+3 & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we selected the positive square root because if $x\ge 3$ is the domain of $f,$ then the range of the inverse is ${f}^{-1}\ge 3.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x)$:

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x-2}+3
$$"] ["question-78fb1a6e-17a5-5dc5-a34e-f2b26dac2b07" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a20ac2fd-f0a8-56d0-b825-05933336bdb3" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*"] [17592186180037 :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, $a=6,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-6)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-6s}\,L\{g(t+6)\},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+6) & =sin\,(7\pi (t+6)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t+42\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡7\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡42\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡7\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡42\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡7\pi t\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡7\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡7\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+6)\} & =L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t)\} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{{s}^{2}+49{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

In our case, we wish to find the transform of

$$

- The shift is $a=3.$

- The shifted function is $f(t-3)=sin\,(2(t-3)).$

$$
f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, we calculate the Laplace transform $F(s)$ of the unshifted function:

$$
F(s)=L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

$$

$$

In our case, we wish to find the transform of

u(t-5){e}^{-4(t-5)}.

By comparing this expression to the form in the theorem, we can identify the following:

- The shift is $a=5.$

- The shifted function is $f(t-5)={e}^{-4(t-5)}.$

From the shifted function, we can deduce the original unshifted function $f(t)$ by simply replacing $(t-5)$ with $t:$

$$
f(t)={e}^{-4t}.
$$

Now, we calculate the Laplace transform $F(s)$ of the unshifted function:

$$
F(s)=L\{{e}^{-4t}\}=\frac{1}{s-(-4)}=\frac{1}{s+4}.
$$

Finally, we apply the shifting theorem formula $L\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\}={e}^{-as}F(s)$ by multiplying $F(s)$ by the exponential delay factor ${e}^{-5s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-5){e}^{-4(t-5)}\} & ={e}^{-5s}\cdot F(s) \\  & ={e}^{-5s}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fe74ebec-be9d-5552-b1e8-03aece81d137" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-02622de9-5ec7-509e-aeaf-23dccc7046e0" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-\frac{1}{3})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\frac{1-y}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{1-y}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{y}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2(\frac{y}{2})}{3} \\  & =\frac{y}{6}.\end{aligned}

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=1-\frac{1}{3}X$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$  Moreover, for $0<x<3,$ we have $0<y<1.$

![](images/af/afe10720ce51bc3dd1b304ea276568d0e505f90159359f5ae54462e4caa729e7.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(1-\frac{X}{3}\le y) \\  & =P(-X\le 3y-3) \\  & =P(X\ge 3-3y) \\  & =1-P(X\le 3-3y) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}(3-3y)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-3)\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(3-3y) \\  & =3\cdot {f}_{X}(3-3y).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =3\cdot {f}_{X}(3-3y) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{9}(3-3y)^{2} \\  & =3{(1-y)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}3{(1-y)}^{2},\, & 0<y<1 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-37fc4f1c-699a-5034-b164-6cf41c6e46b4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5108732e-f4b1-55bf-ab3d-9aaa670d4ed1" :answer-field/id #uuid If $Y={X}^{4},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$"] ["question-670a140c-55d4-5114-b612-9d3a283512c3" :question/worked-solution "To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note  that since the possible values of $X$ are $0<x<1,$ $Y={X}^{4}$ is a strictly increasing function of $X$ when $0<x<1.$ Moreover, for $0<x<1,$ we have $0<y<1.$

![](images/9a/9a6f01a3538711e45e581038af5eaf95e229bf72d08bafefbcf34786a40c1d2d.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{4}\le y) \\  & =P(X\le {y}^{1/4}) \\  & ={F}_{X}({y}^{1/4})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{4{y}^{3/4}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}({y}^{1/4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4{y}^{3/4}}\cdot {f}_{X}({y}^{1/4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{4{y}^{3/4}}\cdot {f}_{X}({y}^{1/4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4{y}^{3/4}}\cdot 2({y}^{1/4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}},\, & 0<y<1 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-670a140c-55d4-5114-b612-9d3a283512c3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-38e37aa3-43fc-561c-9a91-d1b0e6848656" :answer-field/id #uuid - First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that the possible values of $X$ are $x\in (1,\infty ),$ and $Y=\frac{1}{X}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X$ when $X>1.$
 Moreover, for $x>1,$ we have $0<y<1.$

![](images/16/16f3dc78752c8cfcb6b6968e3d57bb3639a4205e2a32dfd569c8c2ca3c29a589.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(\frac{1}{X}\le y) \\  & =P(X\ge \frac{1}{y}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}(\frac{1}{y})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{1}{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{{(\frac{1}{y})}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}1,\, & 0<y<1 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f3a2a8f5-8f7b-5578-9df3-f4e28dce2d10" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ea541e01-5fa9-5c1a-9bd5-70920b6a9e22" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1f799a56-7472-58ef-998d-84e22fb88853" :question/math-academy-id "q-110126"] ["question-1f799a56-7472-58ef-998d-84e22fb88853" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}5{x}^{4},\, & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y=1-{X}^{5},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$"] ["question-1f799a56-7472-58ef-998d-84e22fb88853" :question/worked-solution "To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=1-{X}^{5}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0<x<1,$ we have $0<y<1.$

![](images/05/05534475aecc1d0ebad2234f1259d1b6fd1c6183e47ad763f17c87c5fdb06afb.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(1-{X}^{5}\le y) \\  & =P(-{X}^{5}\le y-1) \\  & =P(X\ge (1-y)^{1/5}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}((1-y)^{1/5})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-\frac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}((1-y)^{1/5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}}\cdot {f}_{X}((1-y)^{1/5}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}}\cdot {f}_{X}((1-y)^{1/5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5(1-y)^{4/5}}\cdot 5{((1-y)^{1/5})}^{4} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}1,\, & 0<y<1 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1f799a56-7472-58ef-998d-84e22fb88853" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-8bffd42c-4c16-5c26-a4d3-ff06e8bcf1b7" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-a4b19843-0372-523c-be3f-e38cf328fccc" :question/math-academy-id "q-110245"] ["question-a4b19843-0372-523c-be3f-e38cf328fccc" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}1,\, & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡X,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$"] ["question-a4b19843-0372-523c-be3f-e38cf328fccc" :question/worked-solution "To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that since the values of $X$ are $0<x<1,$ $Y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡X$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0<x<1,$ we have $y>0.$

![](images/5a/5a2a6f4c5e26819af509e9347fb7aff230927bdd9192ad10a48ce9c951c7be80.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $y>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(-\operatorname{ln}⁡X\le y) \\  & =P(\operatorname{ln}⁡X\ge -y) \\  & =P(X\ge {e}^{-y}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}({e}^{-y})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $y>0,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-{e}^{-y})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}({e}^{-y}) \\  & ={e}^{-y}\cdot {f}_{X}({e}^{-y}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={e}^{-y}\cdot {f}_{X}({e}^{-y}) \\  & ={e}^{-y}\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{-y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y}\, & y>0 \\ 0\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a4b19843-0372-523c-be3f-e38cf328fccc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-f2a17ede-9d12-55e8-9a15-7ee9a3ba31af" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-75b7b0a4-c7ee-525c-b9ca-1a7df7652ed9" :question/math-academy-id "q-110343"] ["question-75b7b0a4-c7ee-525c-b9ca-1a7df7652ed9" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}4{e}^{-4x},\, & x>0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y=-\sqrt[3]{X},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$"] ["question-75b7b0a4-c7ee-525c-b9ca-1a7df7652ed9" :question/worked-solution "To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=-\sqrt[3]{X}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $x>0,$ we have $y<0.$

![](images/4c/4c2b1503e6624c9060829468c9fa0d49856a2d76131975b6b1e437b7de3285c7.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $y<0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt[3]{X}\le y) \\  & =P(-X\le {y}^{3}) \\  & =P(X\ge -{y}^{3}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}(-{y}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $y>0,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-(-3{y}^{2})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-{y}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =3{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{y}^{2}\cdot 4{e}^{-4(-{y}^{3})} \\  & =12{y}^{2}{e}^{4{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}12{y}^{2}{e}^{4{y}^{3}},\, & y<0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-75b7b0a4-c7ee-525c-b9ca-1a7df7652ed9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-98d1d0c4-c915-5b43-86d2-eae585442104" :answer-field/id #uuid Suppose we want to define a new random variable $Y$ as

$$
Y = u(X),
$$

where $u = u(X)$ is a function of $X.$ How do we find the probability density function of $Y?$

To find the PDF of $Y,$ we can use the **distribution function method**. The distribution function method consists of two steps:

- First, we find an expression for $F_Y$ in terms of $F_X,$ where $F_Y$ and $F_X$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate $F_Y$ to get the probability density function $f_Y$ of $Y.$

In this lesson, we'll assume that the function $u$ is strictly monotonic (i.e., strictly increasing or decreasing). The case where $u$ is not monotonic will be dealt with in a future lesson.

![](images/88/88103878042469595fc8f8243958b44b128c0d38465bfe93a31f83afd6988300.svg)
Let $Y= 1+2X.$ Let's use the distribution function method to find the probability density function of $Y.$

First, note that $Y = 1+2X$ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $x > 0,$ we have $y > 1.$

![](images/54/544e551755f4c8a575ef227b77fe520deec203f08654eec31109e496141aa91c.png)

Let's consider $y > 1.$ We write down the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ and then use our transformation to isolate $X$ in the parentheses. This will allow us to write $F_Y$ in terms of $F_X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(2X+1\le y) \\  & =P(2X\le y-1) \\  & =P(X\le \frac{y-1}{2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(\frac{y-1}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $y > 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({F}_{X}(\frac{y-1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{y-1}{2})\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\frac{y-1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\frac{y-1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{y-1}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(\frac{y-1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{-(y-1)/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{(1-y)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{(1-y)/2}, & \,y>1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

It's easy (and often worthwhile) to check that this is a valid probability density function."] [17592186162191 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0] [17592186133620 :question/problem "Given that $(x+2)$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(x)=x^3+2x^2-x-2,$ factor $f(x)$ completely."] [17592186133620 :question/worked-solution "To find the remaining roots, we need to find the other factors of $f(x).$

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |

|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ |
|  | $1$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{x^3 - x^2 - 4x - 2}{x+1} = x^2 - 2x - 2,
$$

$$
x^3 - x^2 - 4x - 2 = (x+1) (x^2 - 2x -2).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $x^2 - 2x - 2$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
\mathcal D = b^2 - 4ac = (-2)^2 - 4(1)(-2) = 12 >     0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $x^2 - 2x - 2$ cannot be factored over the rational numbers since its discriminant is not a perfect square.

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ (over the rational numbers) is given by 

$$
x^3 - x^2 - 4x - 2 = (x+1)(x^2 - 2x - 2).
$$

**Important Note**: Although the quadratic polynomial $(x^2 - 2x - 2)$ does not factor over the rational numbers, it *does* have real roots, because $\mathcal D > 0.$ Therefore, if we were asked to find all of the real roots of $f(x),$ we would need to solve the equations 

$$
x+1 = 0\qquad \textrm{and}\qquad x^2 - 2x - 2 = 0.
$$

The quadratic equation could be solved using the quadratic formula or by completing the square."] ["question-ddb92873-9866-58c6-b7b0-d5953b026f54" :question/id #uuid "ddb92873-9866-58c6-b7b0-d5953b026f54"] ["question-ddb92873-9866-58c6-b7b0-d5953b026f54" :question/math-academy-id "q-40077"] ["question-ddb92873-9866-58c6-b7b0-d5953b026f54" :question/problem "A polynomial $f(x)$ is defined as $f(x)=9{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+7x-1.$ Given that $f(1)=0$, factor $f(x)$ completely."] ["question-ddb92873-9866-58c6-b7b0-d5953b026f54" :question/worked-solution "If $f(1)=0$, then by the factor theorem $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ To factor $f(x)$ we need to find its other factors.

Since $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $9$ | $-15$ | $7$ | $-1$ |
|  | $↓$ | $9$ | $-6$ | $1$ |
|  | $9$ | $-6$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{9{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+7x-1}{x-1}=9{x}^{2}-6x+1,
$$

which means

$$
9{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+7x-1=(x-1)(9{x}^{2}-6x+1).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
(x-1)(9{x}^{2}-6x+1)=(x-1)(3x-1)^{2}.

:question/worked-solution "If $f(4)=0$, then by the factor theorem $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ To factor $f(x)$ we need to find its other factors.

Since $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $2$ | $-15$ | $34$ | $-24$ |
|  | $↓$ | $8$ | $-28$ | $24$ |
|  | $2$ | $-7$ | $6$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+34x-24}{x-4}=2{x}^{2}-7x+6,
$$

which means

$$
2{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}+34x-24=(x-4)(2{x}^{2}-7x+6).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)(2{x}^{2}-7x+6) & =(x-4)(2x-3)(x-2) \\  & =(2x-3)(x-2)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-148f1fdf-ffa7-5ddd-8683-94b6614f6d0f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0ff95e5b-84fb-5fe5-8cb4-3ab8cd0055c1" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1adb95f2-1de2-5cd2-b372-b57ff2f582da" :question/math-academy-id "q-18153"] ["question-1adb95f2-1de2-5cd2-b372-b57ff2f582da" :question/problem "A polynomial $f(x)$ is defined as $f(x)=2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-25x+12.$ Given that $f(3)=0$, what is the sum of the roots of the polynomial?"] ["question-1adb95f2-1de2-5cd2-b372-b57ff2f582da" :question/worked-solution "If $f(3)=0$, then by the factor theorem $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ To find the other roots of the polynomial $f(x)$, we need to find the other factors of $f(x).$

Since $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-3)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned}\enclose{bottom right}{3} & 2 & 1 & -25 & 12 \\  &  & 6 & 21 & -12 \\  & 2 & 7 & -4 & \boxed{0}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-25x+12}{x-3}=2{x}^{2}+7x-4,
$$

which means

$$
2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-25x+12=(x-3)(2{x}^{2}+7x-4).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
(x-3)(2{x}^{2}+7x-4)=(x-3)(2x-1)(x+4).
$$

Now that our polynomial is fully factored, we can see that the three roots of the polynomial are

$$
x=3,\,x=\frac{1}{2},\,x=-4.
$$

Finally, the sum of the roots is

$$
3+\frac{1}{2}-4=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$"] ["question-1adb95f2-1de2-5cd2-b372-b57ff2f582da" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f4776dc4-83d1-5d85-abfe-a8e8c4de2f26" :answer-field/id #uuid Since $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-3)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned}\enclose{bottom right}{3} & 4 & -12 & -1 & 3 \\  &  & 12 & 0 & -3 \\  & 4 & 0 & -1 & \boxed{0}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}-x+3}{x-3}=4{x}^{2}-1,
$$

which means

$$
4{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}-x+3=(x-3)(4{x}^{2}-1).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
(x-3)(4{x}^{2}-1)=(x-3)(2x-1)(2x+1).
$$

Now that our polynomial is fully factored, we can see that the three roots of the polynomial are

$$
x=3,\,x=\frac{1}{2},\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the sum of the roots is

$$

$$"] ["question-349d9aca-faa9-56e3-8806-6dcea184619f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0255dbbb-dbb3-588c-97c7-af1c5b11d4cc" :answer-field/id #uuid root $r$ of a polynomial $p(x),$ then the factor theorem tells us that $(x-r)$ is a factor of $p(x).$ 

For example, if we're given that $x=2$ is a root of the polynomial  $p(x)=x^3-2x^2-x+2,$ then the factor theorem tells us that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

But what if we want to factor the polynomial completely? How can we find the other factors?

The trick is to use division. Because $(x-2)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-2)$ divides $p(x).$ So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-2)$ using synthetic division:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{blue}2$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $2$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-2$ |
|  | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ |

Notice that the remainder turned out to be zero. Whenever we divide a polynomial by one of its factors, we *always* get a remainder of zero.

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{x^3-2x^2-x+2}{x-2}=x^2-1,
$$

which means that

$$
x^3-2x^2-x+2 = (x-2) (x^2-1).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

- the sample size is $n=80,$ and

$$

and

$$

$$

and $n=80$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.42,\frac{0.42(1-0.42)}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0.42,0.003\,045).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.35).$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.35) & =P(Z>\frac{0.35-0.42}{\sqrt{0.003\,045}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-1.27) \\  & =1-P(Z<-1.27) \\  & =1-Φ(-1.27).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.27) & =0.1020.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.35) & =1-Φ(-1.27) \\  & =1-0.1020 \\  & =0.8980.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188684 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186186384 :answer-field/correct 17592186186388] ["question-c3d4715f-79a5-5718-adbc-5959190456a6" :question/id #uuid "c3d4715f-79a5-5718-adbc-5959190456a6"] ["question-c3d4715f-79a5-5718-adbc-5959190456a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-146831"] ["question-c3d4715f-79a5-5718-adbc-5959190456a6" :question/problem "For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

We're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied in each case.

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =50(0.6) \\  & =30 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =50(1-0.6) \\  & =20 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60(0.8) \\  & =48 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60(1-0.8) \\  & =12 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =40(0.9) \\  & =36 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =40(1-0.9) \\  & =4 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $n(1-p)≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\overset{^}{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] ["question-c3d4715f-79a5-5718-adbc-5959190456a6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=80,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.4.$

Now, since

$$
np=80(0.4)=32>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=80(1-0.4)=48>5,
$$

and $n=80$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,0.0030).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $32$ but fewer than $36$ calls are complaints, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{32}{80}<\overset{^}{\,p} & <\frac{36}{80} \\ 0.4\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le 0.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.4<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.45).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.45) & =P(\frac{0.4-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}<Z<\frac{0.45-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<0.91) \\  & =P(Z<0.91)-P(Z<0.00) \\  & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0.00)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.45) & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3b794abe-e844-5b01-84a2-a65b6d920bc6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9fb91e50-0e51-565e-98f0-4e7b44b96808" :answer-field/id #uuid If the newspaper randomly samples $224$ subscribers, find a normal approximation for the probability that between $112$ and $140$ subscribers (inclusive) in the sample have a digital subscription. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

</tbody></table>"] ["question-0c142fbc-f51c-5174-b26c-467ddea21c93" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=224,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{56\,000}{100\,000}=0.56.$

Now, since

$$
np=224(0.56)=125.44>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=224(1-0.56)=98.56>5,
$$

and the $n=224$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,\frac{0.56(1-0.56)}{224}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,0.0011).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $112$ and $140$ of subscribers in the sample have a digital subscription, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{112}{224}\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le \frac{140}{224} \\ 0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p} & \le 0.625.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625) & =P(\frac{0.5-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}\le Z\le \frac{0.625-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.81\le Z\le 1.96) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.96)-P(Z\le -1.81) \\  & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.96)=0.9750,\,Φ(-1.81)=0.0351.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.625) & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81) \\  & =0.9750-0.0351 \\  & =0.9399.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0c142fbc-f51c-5174-b26c-467ddea21c93" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-6a3f931d-2db0-5acf-8977-4c0279c7518b" :answer-field/id #uuid - The first elementary row operation is ${R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={E}_{1}\end{aligned}

- The second elementary row operation is ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={E}_{2}\end{aligned}

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot A
$$

[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot A

:question/problem "Suppose that the following elementary row operations, in the given order, are to be applied to a $2\times 2$ matrix $A:$

$$
{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=6{R}_{2}
$$

Find the equivalent notation in terms of matrix multiplication."] ["question-18af1f73-e41b-5d4c-86dd-e0a8cf91a4f0" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the elementary matrices corresponding to the two given elementary row operations.

- The first elementary row operation is ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={E}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second elementary row operation is ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same  elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={E}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- The third elementary row operation is ${R}_{2}:=6{R}_{2}.$ The corresponding elementary matrix can be found by applying this same elementary row operation to the identity matrix as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:=6{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={E}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To apply the first elementary row operation to the matrix $A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{1}$ on the left and get ${E}_{1}A:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot A
$$

Then, to apply the second elementary row operation to ${E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{2}$ on the left and get ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot A
$$

Finally, to apply the third elementary row operation to ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A,$ we multiply by ${E}_{3}$ on the left and get ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot A
$$"] ["question-18af1f73-e41b-5d4c-86dd-e0a8cf91a4f0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-7d8d06a2-6686-5f9c-8dfb-21558d785068" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-7d8d06a2-6686-5f9c-8dfb-21558d785068"] [17592186115248 :knowledge-point/questions "question-18af1f73-e41b-5d4c-86dd-e0a8cf91a4f0"] [17592186116497 :tutorial/content "To compute the product of an elementary matrix and another matrix, one option is to perform the matrix multiplication as usual. However, there's an easier, quicker way.

Remember that every elementary matrix is the result of applying an elementary row operation to the identity matrix. If we multiply another matrix by an elementary matrix, we're effectively applying the elementary row operation to the other matrix.

For example, suppose we are asked to find the product $EA$ where
![](images/25/25d4c31649834fe3ae42a701d49f6e4a31fa8626de1d9aeed0f98ccbbf4a57fb.svg)

The elementary matrix $E$ comes from swapping the two rows of the identity matrix ($R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$). So, to compute the product $EA,$ all we have to do is swap the two rows of $A\mathbin{:}$
![](images/49/497b76accb211bbe4253ee2094206f70e8856f9510db71f6367f255fcc565665.svg)

This may seem almost too easy. But it's true! And we can verify it by computing the product the long way, using matrix multiplication. Indeed, we get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}EA & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 8 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we say that $E \cdot A$ is equivalent to applying to $A$ the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2.$

**Watch out!** It's important to multiply $A$ from the *left*. If we multiply $A$ by an elementary matrix from the *right*, we will perform a *column* operation on $A$ (not a row operation). In this case, multiplying $A$ by $E$ from the right will have the effect of switching the *columns* of $A,$ not the rows.

$$
\begin{aligned}AE & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 8 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 6 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/id #uuid "01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77"] ["question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/math-academy-id "q-161551"] ["question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/problem "![](images/6e/6e5cb856069061be9b877753ce6c373ee9191547fce8750e9c2a8b073b99ceb0.png)

Given that $R$ is the type II region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V=$"] ["question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/worked-solution "For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](images/e5/e5779dc92c875bef280425ed24a17cfb53f9f2a9736292a92ccdb988044237a6.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{y}^{2}.
$$

![](images/00/00f2847a8e4c927a1c6631f4aef03c57b9d28f18341b268182501ada07225382.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{y}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡z[x]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-01bff6b1-8c04-5993-b5c1-12639cb1fb77" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-25ad75a8-02de-5c76-b6ba-6c420483aaa3" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*"] ["question-688ce6d7-73b6-5ba5-87a1-28b0bc9bdadb" :question/worked-solution "![](images/b7/b7e71e46310b065e2c03b4a0aebaa96268136c7f633eea6983612297e56361d1.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/14/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}12x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}12x\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1+y+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6(1+y+z)^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2}+12yz+12y+12z)\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6z+6{y}^{2}z+2{z}^{3}+6y{z}^{2}+12yz+6{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6+6{y}^{2}+2+6y+12y+6)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+18y+14)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{2}+18y+14)\,dy & =[2{y}^{3}+9{y}^{2}+14y]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(2+9+14)-0 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-688ce6d7-73b6-5ba5-87a1-28b0bc9bdadb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-52c6f404-4a46-5339-9b41-fcaeb9813680" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{4}-4(2)^{3}+7(2)-28 & = \\ 16-32+14-28 & = \\ -30\end{aligned}
$$

III. $u=3$"] ["question-492f172a-6ec8-53da-b873-64a863435b9b" :question/worked-solution "- Substituting $1$ for $u$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{4}-26(1)^{2}+25 & = \\ 1-26(1)+25 & = \\ 1-26+25 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $1$ is substituted for $u.$ Therefore, $1$ is a root.

- Substituting $5$ for $u$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5)^{4}-26(5)^{2}+25 & = \\ 625-26(25)+25 & = \\ 625-650+25 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $5$ is substituted for $u.$ Therefore, $5$ is a root.

- Substituting $3$ for $u$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3)^{4}-26(3)^{2}+25 & = \\ 81-26(9)+25 & = \\ 81-234+25 & = \\ -128\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $3$ is substituted for $u.$ Therefore, $3$ is *not*  a root.

Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{0,2,4\},\,{P}_{2}=\{1,3,5\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the lower Riemann sum $L(f,P).$"] ["question-a55a479e-4a45-5971-8018-f156cd1ee741" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](images/97/97220aa0d23d01e807608e6194a37661ba77cc391d0adf537908c1f13b1b6de8.png)

The lower Riemann sum $L(f,P)$ is given by

$$
L(f,P)={m}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{m}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{m}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{m}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22})
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ is the minimum value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *minimum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *lower* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=4$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $L(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
L(f,P)=4{m}_{11}+4{m}_{21}+4{m}_{12}+4{m}_{22}.
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=9-x-y$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=9-x-y$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](images/30/306666a0e69fca9dc47c2295aa616a944482f00b28fdd96d9d96af816b058447.png)

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion.

![](images/15/15512c5f5063309474534a54b323d87c28cf9b776c10789a8f70e12cdb898aeb.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{11} & =f(2,3)=4 \\ {m}_{21} & =f(4,3)=2 \\ {m}_{12} & =f(2,5)=2 \\ {m}_{22} & =f(4,5)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
L(f,P)=4\cdot 4+4\cdot 2+4\cdot 2+4\cdot 0=32.
$$"] ["question-a55a479e-4a45-5971-8018-f156cd1ee741" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e7df747d-5ae6-580b-89b5-66c235ad174c" :answer-field/id #uuid a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-x=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180029 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-b1c4f06f-dc17-5580-804b-5e960683c34d" :answer/id #uuid "b1c4f06f-dc17-5580-804b-5e960683c34d"] ["question-b2316759-1f4d-59b3-aebb-24c5b1ac8267" :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i-xy\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$"] ["question-b2316759-1f4d-59b3-aebb-24c5b1ac8267" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-xy=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt=du,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}6{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(\frac{1}{4})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }32(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+1}{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+16t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0+32\pi -1)-(0-1) \\  & =32\pi \end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c696854b-d1cc-50f5-8398-3fba96da4739" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b1fc0cd0-57f3-5df9-9d82-31c607584763" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}=8{sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2+x=2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}16{u}^{3}+16u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4696ec15-27d3-55f9-a25e-60bb43e6e055" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d2ae6c02-1c78-5b5d-926b-2d33957e08c9" :answer-field/id #uuid "step-e1f09156-dd59-55de-9346-a705c3bd0957"] [17592186133550 :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $a_n = 8 \cdot 3^n$ for $n\geq 1.$  What is the recursive formula for this sequence?"] [17592186133550 :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_n.
$$

To complete the formula,  we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1.$ The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =8\cdot {3}^{1}=8\cdot 3=24, \\ {a}_{2} & =8\cdot {3}^{2}=8\cdot 9=72.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{72}{24}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric  sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = 3 a_n, \quad a_1 = 24, \quad n \geq 1.
$$"] [17592186133536 :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $f(n) =\dfrac{6}{(-2)^n}$ for $n\geq 1.$  What is the recursive formula for this sequence?"] [17592186133536 :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = r \cdot f(n).
$$

To complete the formula, we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1.$ The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =\frac{6}{(-2)^{1}}=\frac{6}{(-2)}=-3, \\ f(2) & =\frac{6}{(-2)^{2}}=\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{f(2)}{f(1)}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{(-3)}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = -\dfrac{1}{2} f(n), \qquad f(1) = -3, \qquad n \geq 1.
$$"] [17592186133537 :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence

$$
a_{n+1} = 3a_n,\, \qquad a_1 = 1,\, \qquad n\geq 1?
$$"] [17592186133537 :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}, \qquad n \geq 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term $a_1$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1=1.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_n
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r = 3.$

Substituting $a_1 = 1$ and $r = 3$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}	\[5pt]
&= 1 \cdot 3^{n-1} \[5pt]
&= 3^{n-1}.
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=3^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$"] [17592186133551 :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the sequence

$$

$$"] [17592186133551 :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite our recursive formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n+1)=-\frac{f(n)}{3}=-\frac{1}{3}f(n)\end{aligned}
$$

The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n) =f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $f(1)=9.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
f(n+1) = {\color{red}r} \cdot f(n)
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r = -\dfrac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $f(1) = 9$ and $r = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
f(n) &= f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}	\[5pt]
&= 9 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}.
}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =9\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n-1} \\  & =9\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{-1}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n} \\  & =9\cdot (-\frac{3}{1})\cdot {(-\frac{1}{3})}^{n} \\  & =-27\cdot \frac{1}{(-3)^{n}} \\  & =-\frac{27}{(-3)^{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=-\dfrac{27}{(-3)^n} ,\quad n\geq 1.
$$"] ["question-1246524a-95f9-5d04-bcaf-769f77cf931a" :question/id #uuid "1246524a-95f9-5d04-bcaf-769f77cf931a"] ["question-1246524a-95f9-5d04-bcaf-769f77cf931a" :question/math-academy-id "q-251874"] ["question-1246524a-95f9-5d04-bcaf-769f77cf931a" :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is ${a}_{n}=5\cdot {4}^{n}$ for $n\ge 1.$ What is the recursive formula for this sequence? ["question-9a2f8eb3-e0d7-5d85-8fb5-62ab15cba80d" :question/math-academy-id "q-101752"] ["question-9a2f8eb3-e0d7-5d85-8fb5-62ab15cba80d" :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence given by

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{4},\,\,{a}_{1}=-\frac{4}{5},\,\,n\ge 1?
$$"] ["question-9a2f8eb3-e0d7-5d85-8fb5-62ab15cba80d" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1},\,n\ge 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=-\frac{4}{5}.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r=\frac{1}{4}.$

Substituting ${a}_{1}=-\frac{4}{5}$ and $r=\frac{1}{4}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{-1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot \frac{4}{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n} \\  & =-\frac{4\cdot 4}{5\cdot 1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n} \\  & =-\frac{16}{5}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{16}{5}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n},\,n\ge 1.
$$"] ["question-9a2f8eb3-e0d7-5d85-8fb5-62ab15cba80d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-36e03764-6444-5a97-a79c-a332453344e4" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-98925317-9d30-5e69-bd45-e05c5755cffe" :question/math-academy-id "q-44987"] ["question-98925317-9d30-5e69-bd45-e05c5755cffe" :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence given by

$$
{a}_{n+1}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{7},\,\,{a}_{1}=3,\,\,n\ge 1?
$$"] ["question-98925317-9d30-5e69-bd45-e05c5755cffe" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1},\,n\ge 1.
$$

So, we must determine the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is ${a}_{1}=3.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
{a}_{n+1}=r\cdot {a}_{n}
$$

 

From the above, we see that $r=\frac{1}{7}.$

Substituting ${a}_{1}=3$ and $r=\frac{1}{7}$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{1}{7})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =3\cdot {(\frac{1}{7})}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {(\frac{1}{7})}^{-1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{7})}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot 7\cdot (\frac{{1}^{n}}{{7}^{n}}) \\  & =21\cdot \frac{1}{{7}^{n}} \\  & =\frac{21}{{7}^{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{21}{{7}^{n}},\,n\ge 1.
$$"] ["question-98925317-9d30-5e69-bd45-e05c5755cffe" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-723b6e58-02ae-5c02-8cb3-0f391e390f10" :answer-field/id #uuid given the following **explicit formula** for a geometric sequence:

$$
a_n = 2\cdot 5^{n-1}, \qquad n\geq 1
$$

We can write this geometric sequence using a recursive formula. Recall that the recursive formula for *any* geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r\cdot a_n.
$$

To convert from the explicit formula to the recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common ratio. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2\cdot {5}^{0}=2\cdot 1=2 \\ {a}_{2} & =2\cdot {5}^{1}=2\cdot 5=10,\end{aligned}
$$

and the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{10}{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}2}$ and the common ratio is $r={\color{red}5}.$ Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}5} \cdot a_n, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}2}, \qquad n \geq 1
$$"] [17592186135017 :tutorial/content "It's often more useful to translate from the recursive formula to an explicit one. So how do we find the explicit formula for the geometric sequence defined recursively as

$$
a_{n+1} ={\color{red}\dfrac 1 4} a_n,\, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}2},\, \qquad n\geq 1?
$$

The explicit formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1,
$$

so we just need to determine the first term $a_1$ and the common ratio $r.$

We are given that the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}2}.$ To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n+1} & =r\cdot {a}_{n} \\ {a}_{n+1} & =\frac{1}{4}{a}_{n}\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, we see that ${\color{red}r} = {\color{red}\dfrac 1 4}.$

Now we substitute $a_1={\color{blue}2}$ and $r={\color{red}\dfrac{1}{4}}$ into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\eqalign{
a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \
&= {\color{blue}2} \cdot \left( {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{4}} \right)^{n-1}		
}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=2 \cdot \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1.
$$"] [17592186134050 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0] ["question-77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174" :question/id #uuid "77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174"] ["question-77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174" :question/math-academy-id "q-336705"] ["question-77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{7}{3},$ calculate the area (in square units) of $△ABC$ shown above."] ["question-8a507b16-48a7-5e03-967f-cb9296e5eda5" :question/worked-solution "In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{7}{3}.$ Notice that relative to $∠A,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{BC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AC} \\ \frac{7}{3} & =\frac{4x-1}{x+1} \\ 7(x+1) & =3(4x-1) \\ 7x+7 & =12x-3 \\ 7x-12x & =-3-7 \\ -5x & =-10 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =x+1=2+1=3, \\ BC & =4x-1=4(2)-1=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 7 \\  & =10.5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8a507b16-48a7-5e03-967f-cb9296e5eda5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-410ec2bb-6a29-58bd-a046-3457e91665a3" :answer-field/id #uuid Given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{9}{8},$ calculate the area (in square units) of $△ABC$ shown above."] ["question-1bc85b39-7b87-56e7-bb5c-212278f36ea1" :question/worked-solution "In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=\frac{9}{8}.$ Notice that relative to $∠A,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{BC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AC} \\ \frac{9}{8} & =\frac{4x-2}{3x+1} \\ 9(3x+1) & =8(4x-2) \\ 27x+9 & =32x-16 \\ 9+16 & =32x-27x \\ 25 & =5x \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =4x-2=4(5)-2=18, \\ AC & =3x+1=3(5)+1=16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 16\cdot 18 \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1bc85b39-7b87-56e7-bb5c-212278f36ea1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-aab0fb0a-8165-54b3-b1b3-36d377c7585d" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $m∠B={35}^{∘}.$ Notice that relative to $∠B,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{AC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{BC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠B) & =\frac{AC}{BC} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘}) & =\frac{x+2}{2x} \\ 2x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘}) & =x+2 \\ 2x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘})-x & =2 \\ x(2\operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘})-1) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{2\operatorname{tan}⁡({35}^{∘})-1} \\ x & =4.994\,8…\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are 

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =2x=2(4.994\,8…)=9.989\,6…, \\ AC & =x+2=(4.994\,8…)+2=6.994\,8….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}(9.989\,6…)(6.994\,8…) \\  & =34.937\,8… \\  & ≈34.9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place."] ["question-1eaad09e-a27c-5525-b0d1-ca7f3b1ec2af" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1ad64ad7-3b3f-5c5b-8b8e-0a49ed062733" Moreover, for $-2<x<2,$  we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $1\le y<5.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $1\le y<5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}+1\le y) \\  & =P(-(y-1)^{1/2}\le X\le (y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $1\le y<5,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})].\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[\frac{3}{16}{((y-1)^{1/2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{16}{(-(y-1)^{1/2})}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}(\frac{3}{16}(y-1)+\frac{3}{16}(y-1)) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(y-1)^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{y-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{y-1}, & 1\le y<5 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-738870fc-587d-5975-8073-552a681e8d2c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7c65fe3f-7be0-53c6-b431-aa111757d6e5" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-be91f77e-a6ef-5326-b655-78aac371668c" :question/math-academy-id "q-144031"] ["question-be91f77e-a6ef-5326-b655-78aac371668c" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with ![](images/03/03718360bf910c74c22b36f34ad2f63bfad6d9387c0cdc62d3fb366a52f356c9.png)

Moreover, for $-1<x<3,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $0\le y<4.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0\le y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({(1-X)}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}\le 1-X\le {y}^{1/2}) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}-1\le -X\le {y}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =P(1-{y}^{1/2}\le X\le 1+{y}^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0\le y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{1+{y}^{1/2}}{4}+\frac{1-{y}^{1/2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}, & 0\le y<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-be91f77e-a6ef-5326-b655-78aac371668c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c8b4d77c-02ba-56ca-a4f9-ffe483ffd99e" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =2{F}_{X}^{′}(2y+1) \\  & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{8}(2y+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2y+1).\end{aligned}

$$

If the probability density function of $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ is given by
