"Given any vector $\mathbf{x}$ and any subspace $W$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we can always write $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of a vector from $W$ and a vector from $W^{\perp}.$ This fact is known as the **orthogonal decomposition theorem.** We can state it formally as follows:

*Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ can be written uniquely in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}= \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}
$$

where $\mathbf{y} \in W$ and $\mathbf{z} \in W^{\perp}.$* 

*Moreover, since $\mathbf y$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf x$ onto the subspace $W,$ if $\{\mathbf{u}_1\,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}$ is any orthogonal basis of $W,$ then* 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{W}\,x \\  & ={\text{proj}}_{{u}_{1}}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{{u}_{2}}\,x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{u}_{p}}\,x \\  & =\frac{x\cdot {u}_{1}}{{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}}{u}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {u}_{2}}{{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}}{u}_{2}+⋯+\frac{x\cdot {u}_{p}}{{u}_{p}\cdot {u}_{p}}{u}_{p}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "789dc38d-c1e0-5bdc-9f01-5940371a326b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4304 :tutorial/title "The Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "450eea64-01cc-591d-9042-fba21e4feb99" :step/math-academy-id 26173}] :activity/title "The Components of a Vector with Respect to an Orthogonal or Orthonormal Basis" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157482} {:db/id 17592186158103 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158470 :tutorial/content "Given an orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_n\}$ of $S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathcal{B}\},$ there is an easy way to find the components of a vector $\mathbf{x}\in S$ with respect to this basis. $$
B=\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\}\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}$, where ${x}_{i}=\frac{x\cdot {q}_{i}}{{q}_{i}\cdot {q}_{i}}.$ Computing ${x}_{1},$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{x\cdot {q}_{1}}{{q}_{1}\cdot {q}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+4\cdot 2+8\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2+8+8}{1+4+1} \\  & =\frac{18}{6} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

:question/math-academy-id "q-81142" :question/problem "Given the **orthonormal** basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $\sqrt{6}{x}_{2}$, where ${x}_{2}$ is the second component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$
B=\{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{bmatrix}\},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}$, where ${x}_{i}=x\cdot {q}_{i}.$ Computing ${x}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =x\cdot {q}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}+\frac{10}{\sqrt{6}}-\frac{8}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\sqrt{6}{x}_{2}=\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}=6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d60fa14c-dd43-51e9-b0de-5ea532d37c12" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508128}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0990fd7b-21d6-50c6-a747-173db0842535" :answer/type {:db/id Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186305099 :question/id #uuid "f20c0d44-466d-592f-adfd-5535d1164b77" :question/math-academy-id "q-332705"} {:db/id 17592186305100 :question/id #uuid Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-4t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2196ea04e12f3c706300e0c9d15806606e408f5e582d3e4f2b9c62f0efc343f.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-2t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-2{c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/24/2473117cdca4318187b94374820c0a12576e998e7f631a6e7bf51e56c985be43.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{6t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{6{c}_{1}{e}^{6t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{7t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/96/96801605aa5d777eb18c13ded1f7b7e59ae74968b210da3b7a26f339a1c9f673.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{7t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{7t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{3t})^{′}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}}{3{c}_{1}{e}^{3t}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=9$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{9t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{9t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

![](images/99/99d6e9894c7117c5684e17702540d0eb469b6e824381cf2263c843f8f55ee8d8.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{9t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{9{c}_{1}{e}^{9t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{9{c}_{1}}{e}^{-5t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable node (sink)}.$

:topic/math-academy-id 3242} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167843 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167997 :tutorial/content "Consider a *decoupled* linear system of ODEs
![](images/3f/3f7a114fa75100f8cd3ccf72822758e668f3a6a0824ad5f5437ebef138928fb5.svg)

In this lesson, we consider only decoupled systems with nonzero eigenvalues ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/b8/b8ed089264b88bdcf4018f44db6dade448063b56a6ded558fb74d7c2ca61c0de.svg) so the origin is the equilibrium point we will classify.

Recall that the eigenvalues for a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/af/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) 
The corresponding eigenvectors are parallel to the coordinate axes:
![](images/83/8337ebfc4aae4b8e97438cdba58872082bdc8965932659fdf2f8ff9cf061b375.svg)

So, the general solution of the system is given by
![](images/fc/fcb5c1cea49dfe7aa1058f64d859a8b47c363f7f6195bf68056b18f1fa6d37f2.svg)

Notice that if a solution starts on one of the coordinate axes, it remains on that axis. These are called **straight-line solutions**:

- On the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis (![](images/8d/8da7ef7a61d4c5af4d28575fcd263714cf3bda8e7d94985bd4bea5c03eb2d53f.svg)): 
![](images/aa/aa9cd3c49609ee6d09a61c9c31438e4297620feedfda1073fbc55c08e7c53d01.svg)

- On the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis (![](images/f2/f271ee76900762067d886b30871a9ea7538ae69318ad4514e5b39cfdce12644b.svg)):
![](images/50/509154a662b215d445b282396a8f43828e582d43282467a0da73843ade7ec5d8.svg)

The stability of these solutions as ![](images/91/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the *signs* of the eigenvalues ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/af/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) We will explore the three main stability cases in the upcoming examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "3ab2b715-abcc-511c-bbda-a2664d39efda" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14436 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a60bbebf-7d50-57b0-b823-f5cde68f6ecb" :step/math-academy-id 588112 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167852}} {:db/id 17592186167844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168002 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.$ 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/75/75e7a0e16141db2a8da210c1ab30fc7328ccc98f861afec4db69d951ff3c9121.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/28/280e99a308962d43d1060be7100e294623d3bc3bfbe0579ab61d817695ad9e45.svg) Since $\lambda_2>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

Because both axes are *unstable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an **unstable node** or **source**.

In the phase portrait, we draw:

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), and

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin).

A typical trajectory for an *unstable node* emanates from the origin toward infinity. 

![](images/c9/c9f315c0b8a60a2c00e2f8e8e8b954214ce4d82cfd5832e15c26b429e29e535e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "302544e8-9eeb-5087-ae71-7143ffcbad9f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14460 :tutorial/title "Both Positive Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "752fcd7d-e772-51d0-84f5-e0724d157464" :step/math-academy-id 588113 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167845}} {:db/id 17592186167845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168003 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

where ![](images/78/7853d8d4de1afb7f8899c60d7a5ea8e5ecd281594e48536c9f2d0bbef2c0301b.svg)

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis have the form ![](images/a1/a12ab1d3c69a589aa8de66fe8d14ed19b2938a9ef5591d87860e101a95afdc55.svg) Since ![](images/3d/3db8d2103adafd2be29df482295b07ef63576be6f152793463e034e808725edf.svg) we have that ![](images/bb/bb6223675110a379d33203ff637afaa6aefd3edf507b5a93386c608aa7aafca5.svg) as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) Thus, the trajectories on the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis move *toward* the origin (*stable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis have the form ![](images/aa/aae0f8015e0a575ca1e1fdbb37d011cbf78574649e3c9874163c3f14f1ca9929.svg) Since ![](images/23/23d0a8291d49cc1d2f0c6cff735a4d5214c2d9079dca67d803846af9b063358f.svg) we have that ![](images/69/69c464920e94e968ac5b2fe07f52d5e8a5e694f0fab6c9bfdcfd1b359a82e89e.svg) as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) Thus, the trajectories on the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis move *toward* the origin (*stable axis*).

Because both axes are *stable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **stable node** or **sink**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin), and

- arrows on the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory flows into the origin.

![](images/df/df904ec5214399987c94f99323d3c3c4c06d9e19242c0d580574488011475acc.svg)
we know the *signs* of ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/c0/c0413ea28006ddd6542ba7f9ebf2714b6091aca8fa79396d545b48db347c3a80.svg) tell us the type of the equilibrium (sink/source/saddle). But how can we determine the shape of trajectories in cases when the origin is a source (![](images/bb/bb6302eab08feb0614c62d4ea8012676675715a469dd30a7321ec228ff7ef4e9.svg)) or a sink (![](images/be/be8860e40a1c229262d3bf3375732f4b4583cad7aaf63f3a17e871bbd5a51abb.svg))?

To do this, we can compare the rates of change of ![](images/f7/f7dbfa03976240534a1b57f2cc59c474401a0d9524bc5f627736da01a0d775c1.svg) and ![](images/cc/cc436bde605f3822acb66d36528ba42a812a50fdbea361b31f0dbd0cba61d810.svg) by looking at the slope of the tangent line to the trajectory, ![](images/c7/c7244a31f756199a29c0e7e755eccdf9274346e643e0856566469b35a207e53a.svg) Assuming ![](images/37/371aec72d3e326e3e52fbd1a1cfc06be06b33e3054e60b8c286a9fcbac39141e.svg) we have:
![](images/be/be21baf0c518d85b105b0f569382fbc47075c268847437046b042db36a9b4b8a.svg)

As we can see, the long-term behavior of the slope as ![](images/91/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the sign of the exponent, ![](images/7c/7cde6653feb562f0d136150bffa6f2925af0c7dbcb9ede5c7f1b3e0f10f3796d.svg)

This comparison is governed by which eigenvalue is larger. We call the larger eigenvalue (the one that is more positive, or less negative) the **dominant eigenvalue**.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186167851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166915 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166540 :question/id #uuid "4926ad20-fc6b-5a7d-80ee-aa39421c174d" :question/math-academy-id "e-21607"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "24bd917d-c4b3-5bf5-9426-a87a579b03c1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167200} {:db/id 17592186167236} {:db/id 17592186308409} {:db/id 17592186308410} {:db/id 17592186308411} {:db/id 17592186391158} {:db/id 17592186391169} {:db/id 17592186420019} {:db/id 17592186420021} {:db/id 17592186420025} {:db/id 17592186444147}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations"} :step/id #uuid "6cadc020-1f0c-5e3d-88b7-c3977e63cc74" :step/math-academy-id 588126} {:db/id 17592186167852 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186168004 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

"![](images/aa/aaeba63f6237121fe226eb30e5378d3e93129bb2782b9c8acb8d73ac719676b3.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0f0eb2d5-220a-51b8-8ecc-e34f70d2ec6c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444151}} {:db/id 17592186444151 :step/content {:db/id 17592186391144 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6095321f-3c3a-5564-bd76-8ac789465110" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/63/635e8687fbccc7612f692ec1a1abaa9802bafe9c3773e4b0c058a18813e7249e.png" :db/id 17592186391146} {:answer/id #uuid "9f24dea2-7b89-5ce9-93de-ca7b97049c38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/a5/a5ae215022638430d0c89dddd97c01ae7598b6251bd013ef48ca9771029b8cd6.png" :db/id 17592186391147} {:answer/id #uuid "f70a8ce1-5b6e-5473-90f3-bf87bae67685" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/c9/c9816edf7fb99b759361abc4333f3ed0d3676d2c77db2210367466b66837bca8.png" :db/id 17592186391148} {:answer/id #uuid "9fcceae6-4fa4-5965-9386-71fc659c0936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/c4/c497d1f9dd6cb5bc473bd46ec56c465228408447fb2436b80f16a23b282654b2.png" :db/id 17592186391149} {:answer/id #uuid "65324022-a078-5bdb-b4aa-e0381dbb7e37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/4f/4f613e414cdb619a9b09f25a47b7e4cad953440c40d91f876322d7e1cb59b8c4.png" :db/id 17592186391150}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186391149} :answer-field/id #uuid "41bd2e0d-7517-5053-bcbd-08e7df5307b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186391145}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "34a4a204-b6f5-559d-8b71-d224e42d358b" :question/math-academy-id "q-333177" :question/problem "$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=9$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{9t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{9t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/99/99d6e9894c7117c5684e17702540d0eb469b6e824381cf2263c843f8f55ee8d8.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{9t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{9{c}_{1}{e}^{9t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{9{c}_{1}}{e}^{-5t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

"q-333222" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=3y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.

$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=9$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{9t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{9t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/99/99d6e9894c7117c5684e17702540d0eb469b6e824381cf2263c843f8f55ee8d8.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{9t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{9{c}_{1}{e}^{9t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{9{c}_{1}}{e}^{-5t}.\end{aligned}

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2c81ff3c50013c149dc6a5db67bbe11cccdbbef22ce2c0712101f4a358bcb8c.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form

lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-7y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1686fe8b-2f6a-5497-b24c-e3b125e58c6d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534124}} {:db/id 17592186534116 :step/content {:db/id 17592186420021 :question/answer-fields {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/24/2473117cdca4318187b94374820c0a12576e998e7f631a6e7bf51e56c985be43.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{6t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{6{c}_{1}{e}^{6t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{7t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/96/96801605aa5d777eb18c13ded1f7b7e59ae74968b210da3b7a26f339a1c9f673.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{7t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{7t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{3t})^{′}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}}{3{c}_{1}{e}^{3t}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=6x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/24/2473117cdca4318187b94374820c0a12576e998e7f631a6e7bf51e56c985be43.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{6t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{6{c}_{1}{e}^{6t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$

$$

with respect to $x$ at  $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186540068 :question/id #uuid "8b961be3-a61d-5fd5-a33f-daa3b859082d" :question/math-academy-id "q-276044" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "abd7469e-6019-5f0b-8db1-f38b3d8887b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186539770}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539770} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1453ef1-7ffc-594f-a954-83c62ec2f697" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186540003} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fbd51744-3817-5b56-83ea-b6c1a15c1145" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186539904}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539904} :answer-field/id #uuid "e69fbcb6-2b3e-5e04-95d1-2af8c246cb30" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186540006}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 0-10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186208848 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186208272 :question/id #uuid "fce0099e-b010-50a4-bf0d-51aca4380129" :question/math-academy-id "e-17865"} :knowledge-point/id :db/id 17592186205341}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot y \\  & ={A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186532646 :question/id #uuid "411aabaa-bd7a-5b74-b0d5-19adca16cb89" :question/math-academy-id "q-269470"} {:db/id 17592186532648 :question/id #uuid "41cc5d66-bf23-517e-b32a-3cd7a74b1b32" :question/math-academy-id "q-269549"} {:db/id 17592186532704 :question/id #uuid "c92e05a7-340f-573b-9fe1-3137e228de5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-269518"} {:db/id 17592186532708 :question/id #uuid "d5a5695b-8296-5985-af65-b20134a9d8cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-269465"} {:db/id 17592186540048 :question/id #uuid "3f634cb0-d91f-55a0-8036-9bf4e6795f5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-269525" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "263e9c79-2b5d-5fc6-ae10-bec804651dad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}30 \\ 42\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539553} {:answer/id #uuid "5e6bef22-fee1-53f1-8d0f-2529ad295f2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}30 & 42\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539639} {:answer/id #uuid "85ee42d0-6b46-5068-8546-0b6d45122f68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}21 \\ 15\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539700} {:answer/id #uuid "a2df55cc-4d93-55a0-9838-4a5a0b419174" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}58 & 26\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539752} {:answer/id #uuid "ae374fd7-8d71-5715-bb99-e0fa0ee5417f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539776}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539776} :answer-field/id #uuid "a4ae1559-7267-51e9-bbdf-d599082e8f60" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539977}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-2b)^{T}(Ax-2b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-2b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048550} {:answer-field/id #uuid "9dbcc980-616b-5303-845b-f45d71fb4019" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186205482} {:answer-field/id #uuid "a1b6b2b9-cab1-5fb2-a850-af253412d9f6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186205483} {:answer-field/id #uuid "a724e81f-55cf-58b5-a654-69095d3cecb6" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186205484} {:activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186209870} :activity/id #uuid "e03cea40-d542-50a2-beef-0257307c0a4f" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050484 :topic/id #uuid "4d4dd9cc-d32a-5514-bbc8-b9d4357f3376" :topic/math-academy-id 6007} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186209870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209878 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of gradients of scalar functions to include quadratic functions, quadratic forms, and the chain rule.

Consider the (scalar) **quadratic function**

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a matrix, and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n$ is a column vector. We wish to calculate the gradient of this function:

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf x} f = \nabla_{\mathbf x} \left(\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}\right)
$$

We start by showing that $f$ can be written in the expanded form 

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

To understand why this is the same as $\mathbf x^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf x,$ let's first write
![](images/39/394b4241f76616fae493bcc281cbe782c1d1a89680ef24cd2776c02302b9550d.svg)

Now, we compute $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$ by working step by step.

First, we compute the product $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$, which gives us an $n\times 1$ column vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & ⋯ & {a}_{1n} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & ⋯ & {a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {a}_{n1} & {a}_{n2} & ⋯ & {a}_{nn}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}{x}_{1}+{a}_{12}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{1n}{x}_{n} \\ {a}_{21}{x}_{1}+{a}_{22}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{2n}{x}_{n} \\ ⋮ \\ {a}_{n1}{x}_{1}+{a}_{n2}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{nn}{x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{1j}{x}_{j} \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{2j}{x}_{j} \\ ⋮ \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{nj}{x}_{j}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply $\mathbf{x}^T$ by this result:
![](images/15/15180b9898708fa3f2398a534c0e4f0a57f4466abd046b388eb7af3009e534b0.svg)

Each term of this product looks like $x_i \cdot \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_j$, so the full expression becomes

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \left( \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_j \right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

So, we've shown that

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.}
$$

Let's now discuss how this helps us to compute the gradient of $f.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "46d7287c-3842-57d9-8f8b-8f5f95c5362f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12386 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b43433a0-9dff-53f0-b8cf-64336b4b2fc7" :step/math-academy-id 610963 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209871}} {:db/id 17592186209871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209954 :tutorial/content "We have the quadratic function

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}
$$

where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a matrix, and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n$ is a column vector. As we've seen, $f$ can be written in the expanded form

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

We'll use this form to compute the gradient of $f.$

To compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f$, we'll differentiate this expanded form with respect to $x_k.$ First, we express our expanded function as

$$
f(\mathbf x) =  \sum_{i \neq k} \sum_{j \neq k} A_{ij} x_i x_j 
+ \sum_{i \neq k} A_{ik} x_i x_k 
+ \sum_{j \neq k} A_{kj} x_k x_j 
+ A_{kk} x_k^2.
$$

The idea here is to break up the double summation by isolating all the terms that involve the variable $x_k$. 

Notice that

- the first summation is *independent* of $x_k,$

- the second and third summations are *linear* in $x_k,$ and

- the final term is *quadratic* in $x_k.$

We can now compute our derivative term by term in a structured way. Differentiating with respect to $x_k,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{k}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{k}}[{\sum }_{i\ne k}{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}+{\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}{x}_{k}+{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{k}{x}_{j}+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k}^{2}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}+{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j}+2{A}_{kk}{x}_{k} \\  & =({\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i})+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k}+({\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j})+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j} \\  & =({A}^{T}x)_{k}+(Ax)_{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is true for all $1\leq k \leq n$, we get the result

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}) = A^T \mathbf{x} + A \mathbf{x} = (A^T + A)\mathbf x.
$$

From here, we have the following special cases:

- If $A$ is symmetric, then $A^T = A,$ $f(\mathbf x)$ is a quadratic form, and our result simplifies to

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}) = 2 A \mathbf{x}.
$$

- Suppose that $A = I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. Then, our result for symmetric matrices simplifies to

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T  \mathbf{x}) = 2 \mathbf{x}
$$

which is a result we saw in a previous lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "332e4bab-6a1d-5868-a616-4a2c034c2619" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13115 :tutorial/title "The Gradient of a Quadratic Function"} :step/id #uuid "b7685ad5-7aa7-532e-936b-bd0ad89e40bd" :step/math-academy-id 610964 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209872}} {:db/id 17592186209872 :step/content {:db/id 17592186208846 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186208271 :question/id #uuid "a06524d0-6980-52eb-b5fb-2ca7d0c1dbac" :question/math-academy-id "e-17350"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9fe0d364-ef22-5138-9ee5-e473bd909447" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048851} {:db/id 17592186049450}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186208924} {:db/id 17592186208925} {:db/id 17592186532650} {:db/id 17592186532661} {:db/id 17592186532671} {:db/id 17592186532724} {:db/id 17592186540069}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Form"} :step/id #uuid "1f3213b1-5ea3-5cd6-9b86-84bd1ef095b3" :step/math-academy-id 610965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209873}} {:db/id 17592186209873 :step/content {:db/id 17592186208847 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186208289 :question/id #uuid "b4e84c40-15d1-585f-84c7-c615979cd8f5" :question/math-academy-id "e-18713"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2198cf08-3a99-5e5d-80af-bbe722b51647" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186208956} {:db/id 17592186208957} {:db/id 17592186532652} {:db/id 17592186532660} {:db/id 17592186532689} {:db/id 17592186532692} {:db/id 17592186540057} {:db/id 17592186540068}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Function"} :step/id #uuid "bc662f29-b540-527e-bb28-752fc9820d44" :step/math-academy-id 610968 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209874}} {:db/id 17592186209874 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209877 :tutorial/content "Now, let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $f: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}$. Suppose we want to compute the gradient 

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})).
$$

To do this, we need to apply the chain rule. The chain rule for total derivatives tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{1 \times n}
= 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{1 \times q}
\cdot 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Now, recall that the gradient of a scalar function is the transpose of the total derivative:

$$
\underbrace{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f}_{n \times 1} = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
$$

To derive the chain rule in terms of gradients, we apply the identity $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={{{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{n\times q}\cdot {{{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{q\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient chain rule is

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
\cdot 
\nabla_{\mathbf{y}} f.
$$

Note that the order matters; when expressed in the gradient form, the derivatives are applied *from right to left!*" :tutorial/id #uuid "eb90df7d-906c-5d50-a61a-40222511f26e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12301 :tutorial/title "Computing Gradients With the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "42b51395-66f8-5f41-b3b6-f3e548175320" :step/math-academy-id 610971 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209875}} {:db/id 17592186209875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186208848 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186208272 :question/id #uuid "fce0099e-b010-50a4-bf0d-51aca4380129" :question/math-academy-id "e-17865"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0c77271f-3d21-5193-a1ad-5c0264e337f0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048367}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186208929} {:db/id 17592186208930} {:db/id 17592186532646} {:db/id 17592186532648} {:db/id 17592186532704} {:db/id 17592186532708} {:db/id 17592186540048}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Chain Rule to Gradients"} :step/id #uuid "2a7727ac-4542-5d23-af4c-7a22c6bc3047" :step/math-academy-id 610972}] :activity/title "Further Vector Gradients" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186208872} {:db/id 17592186209870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209878 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of gradients of scalar functions to include quadratic functions, quadratic forms, and the chain rule.

f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

We'll use this form to compute the gradient of $f.$

To compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f$, we'll differentiate this expanded form with respect to $x_k.$ First, we express our expanded function as

$$
f(\mathbf x) =  \sum_{i \neq k} \sum_{j \neq k} A_{ij} x_i x_j 
+ \sum_{i \neq k} A_{ik} x_i x_k 
+ \sum_{j \neq k} A_{kj} x_k x_j 
+ A_{kk} x_k^2.
$$

The idea here is to break up the double summation by isolating all the terms that involve the variable $x_k$. 

Notice that

- the first summation is *independent* of $x_k,$

- the second and third summations are *linear* in $x_k,$ and

- the final term is *quadratic* in $x_k.$

We can now compute our derivative term by term in a structured way. Differentiating with respect to $x_k,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{k}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{k}}[{\sum }_{i\ne k}{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}+{\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}{x}_{k}+{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{k}{x}_{j}+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k}^{2}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}+{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j}+2{A}_{kk}{x}_{k} \\  & =({\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i})+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k}+({\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j})+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j} \\  & =({A}^{T}x)_{k}+(Ax)_{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is true for all $1\leq k \leq n$, we get the result

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}) = A^T \mathbf{x} + A \mathbf{x} = (A^T + A)\mathbf x.
$$

From here, we have the following special cases:

- If $A$ is symmetric, then $A^T = A,$ $f(\mathbf x)$ is a quadratic form, and our result simplifies to

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}) = 2 A \mathbf{x}.
$$

- Suppose that $A = I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. Then, our result for symmetric matrices simplifies to

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T  \mathbf{x}) = 2 \mathbf{x}
$$

Suppose we want to compute the gradient 

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})).
$$

To do this, we need to apply the chain rule. The chain rule for total derivatives tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{1 \times n}
= 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{1 \times q}
\cdot 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Now, recall that the gradient of a scalar function is the transpose of the total derivative:

$$
\underbrace{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f}_{n \times 1} = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
$$

To derive the chain rule in terms of gradients, we apply the identity $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={{{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{n\times q}\cdot {{{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{q\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient chain rule is

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
\cdot 
\nabla_{\mathbf{y}} f.
$$

Note that the order matters; when expressed in the gradient form, the derivatives are applied *from right to left!*" :tutorial/id #uuid "eb90df7d-906c-5d50-a61a-40222511f26e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12301 :tutorial/title "Computing Gradients With the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "42b51395-66f8-5f41-b3b6-f3e548175320" :step/math-academy-id 610971 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209875}} {:db/id 17592186209877 :tutorial/content "Now, let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $f: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}$. "6d939167-bbdf-5642-a79d-3234f69c9c09" :question/math-academy-id "q-276043" :question/problem "Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x
$$

with respect to $x$ at  $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3eaf924d-cd34-5820-a14e-44d3eca661aa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186540134}} {:db/id 17592186540134 :step/content {:db/id 17592186540068 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "abd7469e-6019-5f0b-8db1-f38b3d8887b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186539770}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539770} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1453ef1-7ffc-594f-a954-83c62ec2f697" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186540003} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fbd51744-3817-5b56-83ea-b6c1a15c1145" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186539904}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539904} :answer-field/id #uuid "e69fbcb6-2b3e-5e04-95d1-2af8c246cb30" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186540006}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8b961be3-a61d-5fd5-a33f-daa3b859082d" :question/math-academy-id "q-276044" :question/problem "Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by
