$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 0-10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "44fdf552-67f4-506b-8352-bf3ff777ad37"} {:db/id 17592186540149 :step/content {:db/id 17592186208930 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0288d1c8-90da-55c4-98e8-5a5eabefe8cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 22\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539481} {:answer/id #uuid "86d96929-a573-5ba1-a568-15337e2bcf56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-7 & -29\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539703} {:answer/id #uuid "cc83261d-2254-5227-8497-098b5fbcaed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539828} {:answer/id #uuid "e136544d-ec3c-563b-b13e-653feae14454" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 & 22\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539864} {:answer/id #uuid "ff114911-6bea-5d83-a4a0-4820ac877a2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}25 \\ -11\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186539914}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539828} :answer-field/id #uuid "6839df18-40b0-55d8-b0ee-244e7c3bdebb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186205341}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8b2d453b-0edb-52e1-a8ad-599845d2374a" :question/math-academy-id "q-269515" :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$L(x)=(Ax-2b)^{T}(Ax-2b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-2b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ac05d334-16c5-5e79-9fe0-8447dbb842a5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186540132}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "110945c0-e65b-5532-b050-4bd230c8fb1d" :answer/type {:db/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186493969 :question/id #uuid "dfba6eb1-d0b6-5cbc-ac16-d682a2e1cc93" :question/math-academy-id "q-95286" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08b31b5f-4d45-56bb-9d27-10f181056843" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186493405} {:answer/id #uuid "1f5ebfbd-349c-5710-ab1d-bffdb6d4d025" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493445} {:answer/id #uuid "21c0505d-1159-59fb-ba8b-2bd5ac4199de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493447} {:answer/id #uuid "94c66a12-70a7-529f-ba21-ac7f034b13c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493623} {:answer/id #uuid "e4ada2c6-ebf0-5d58-9a21-8f0d7d2bddb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493752}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493447} :answer-field/id #uuid "6457d0d0-1968-5324-849a-7bcaae3a3d7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493831}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ 16-2\lambda -8\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -10) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{10} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186184877 :question/id #uuid "e9152817-159b-5a54-868d-fe52d19640cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-94981" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a7d4ed93-75bb-5db0-9900-2362979d6c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4,\,3,\,0" :db/id 17592186404734} {:answer/id #uuid "aac056f1-2c7a-51fc-b3b8-c7516856527b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404735} {:answer/id #uuid "2ef4562a-20e9-5af5-80a4-ced17b367b83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404736} {:answer/id #uuid "fd4157e7-a2cf-562a-af6a-fea80f5a7f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16,\,9,\,0" :db/id 17592186404737} {:answer/id #uuid "95d80c78-37a1-5b82-8b12-a47780191024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9,\,4,\,0" :db/id 17592186404738}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404735} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce3dc232-fc1d-50e4-99b4-15ed1b8fa187" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404733}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4-\lambda  \\ -2 & -4\end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(20-4\lambda -5\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186367540 :question/id #uuid "a7d5c241-f1dd-539c-bc82-e319298f04d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-139500" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11f72538-1df2-5400-9f78-cb8409f95ed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$5$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186367542} {:answer/id #uuid "aaed5f82-08d1-5931-9dc0-ef6782cb00fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$4$ and $3$" :db/id 17592186367543} {:answer/id #uuid "85459f08-ebd2-5de2-af01-144d2aeb100c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$5$ and $1$" :db/id 17592186367544} {:answer/id #uuid "d4be0251-97f5-5981-bda6-e62b677f0ba2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$5$ and $4$" :db/id 17592186367545} {:answer/id #uuid "c7dc7fb6-4c25-5dc1-b337-7a9abd5eaf65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$4$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186367546}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367544} :answer-field/id #uuid "2b11b93b-5ed4-5c27-8e1f-ae8a252505fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367541}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}13 & 12 \\ 12 & 13\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}13-\lambda  & 12 \\ 12 & 13-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (13-\lambda )(13-\lambda )-144 & =0 \\ 169-26\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-144 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-26\lambda +25 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368920 :question/id #uuid "80bd1a5b-eef3-57d3-b7a8-ea1d67708737" :question/math-academy-id "q-95364" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186184198 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2bf7196-b681-5ff6-bf16-24acefa04e6c" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17453e7d-2501-500c-988d-632cc6dfbc65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$4$ and $0$" :db/id 17592186368922} {:answer/id #uuid "3e7fa423-ce11-5e4b-941d-b20daa102519" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$8$ and $4$" :db/id 17592186368923} {:answer/id #uuid "7cf839ad-4dca-5536-a5e6-2102abbf3175" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$8$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186368924} {:answer/id #uuid "d0871187-035d-52b5-b781-f70eaa3bf24c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$4$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186368925} {:answer/id #uuid "0183a8ef-a247-5fec-a72f-23430bb57861" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$2$ and $1$" :db/id 17592186368926}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "d0871187-035d-52b5-b781-f70eaa3bf24c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$4$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186368925} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbd50738-594a-50f0-9455-2e79aec8430d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186368921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}10-\lambda  & -6 \\ -6 & 10-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(10-\lambda )-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +100-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +64 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =16,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :tutorial/id #uuid "6230f35e-b526-5e84-be30-86c8cdcbd301" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}10-\lambda  & -6 \\ -6 & 10-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(10-\lambda )-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +100-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +64 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =16,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "65534646-ddcd-5bd8-a87f-2133012193c1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508123}} {:db/id 17592186508145 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184877 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a7d4ed93-75bb-5db0-9900-2362979d6c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4,\,3,\,0" :db/id 17592186404734} {:answer/id #uuid "aac056f1-2c7a-51fc-b3b8-c7516856527b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404735} {:answer/id #uuid "2ef4562a-20e9-5af5-80a4-ced17b367b83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404736} {:answer/id #uuid "fd4157e7-a2cf-562a-af6a-fea80f5a7f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16,\,9,\,0" :db/id 17592186404737} {:answer/id #uuid "95d80c78-37a1-5b82-8b12-a47780191024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9,\,4,\,0" :db/id 17592186404738}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404735} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce3dc232-fc1d-50e4-99b4-15ed1b8fa187" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404733}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e9152817-159b-5a54-868d-fe52d19640cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-94981" :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$  

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

The smallest positive value of $c$ that has this property is called the **period** of the function.

Let's take the following periodic function as an example:

![](images/f4/f483c51678bf15e97f1891d95ed9dda7e697ef18a593a507171a45e6cc7ffc7e.png)

This function repeats itself with a period of $2$. To illustrate, first focus on the part of the graph shown in blue below.

![](images/fb/fbba2663aaca4514f0b6132ed36e48d7568637fe0faac327d6935b5f5df65541.png)

If we shift this part $2$ units to the right, the graph remains unchanged!

![](images/de/deeadebca74eb6e466ebb13240e8f4cf9b0d2c03fedb5f8a94be18f1ddcd44f1.png)

The same would happen if we shifted the part $2$ units to the left.

By knowing the period of a periodic function, we can use a value of the function to infer many other values of the function. For example, in the function above, note that

$$
f(4)=0
$$

Since the period is $2$, if we add (or subtract) any multiple of $2$ from the input, the output stays the same. We can write this as

$$
f(4+2n) = 0
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

For example, setting

$$
n=1,2,3\ldots
$$

gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n = 1: f(4 + 2(1)) &= f(6) = 0 \\
n = 2: f(4 + 2(2)) &= f(8) = 0 \\
n = 3: f(4 + 2(3)) &= f(10) = 0 \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

The same is true for negative values of $n$. Setting

$$
n=-1,-2,-3\ldots
$$

gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n =-1: f(4 + 2(-1)) &= f(2) = 0 \\
n =-2: f(4 + 2(-2)) &= f(0) = 0 \\
n =-3: f(4 + 2(-3)) &= f(-2) = 0 \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}

principal axes of the curve $19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2 = 20.$" :question/worked-solution "First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=19x_1^2-6x_1x_2+11x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is 

![](images/31/31f8c54fecdb8b2e8b3f3cad20a642a39eab9ae2987d49849a1c1dabc34e5368.png)

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 20
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=20 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=10.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_2=20,$ we have

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=48
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}+1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=2
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

:tutorial/content "Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables 

$$
\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}
$$

that transforms the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ into the quadratic form $\mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. 

The columns of the matrix $P$ are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of $A,$ which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the **principal axes** of the quadratic form.

Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation 

$$
6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,
$$

and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

![](images/d8/d8a6b6dff52e0c4004432f9447b5fd484612eaacf07588c3469af143b0a9e880.png)

It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,
$$

which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

So, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +14 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

$\qquad$ $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$

Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes $y_1$ and $y_2.$ 

![](images/10/10a2f0ccd179eba7f65410f932548d954a459e1bc8dcb0803a5b2d9fe7896432.png)

In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to 

$$
7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.
$$

 

Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2} & =14 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{7}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2f9d7d81-cc50-5024-8f69-3b529968aeac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4890 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :step/next {:db/id 17592186162901}} {:db/id 17592186162938 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163256 :tutorial/content "In some special cases, a quadratic equation might generate a degenerate curve or even an empty set.

- For example, consider the quadratic equation 

$$
-3x_1^2+8x_1x_2+3x_2^2 = 0.
$$

Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain

$$
5y_1^2 - 5y_2^2 = 0
$$

which represents two intersecting lines $y_1 = y_2$ and $y_1 = -y_2.$

- Now consider the quadratic equation 

$$
-2x_1^2+8x_1x_2-8x_2^2 = 10.
$$

Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain

$$
- 10y_2^2 =10
$$

which represents an empty set as the equation $y_2^2 = -1$ does not have any real solution.

- Finally, reducing the left-hand side of 

$$
x_1^2-4x_1x_2+4x_2^2 = 5
$$

to the canonical form, we obtain

$$
5y_2^2 =5
$$

which represents a pair of parallel lines $y_2 = 1$ and $y_2=-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cf07f443-3757-578e-908a-51eaef4cde16" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5077 :tutorial/title "Some Special Cases"} :step/id #uuid "2d3c6630-85aa-524d-9982-1c2a440c6b5f" :step/math-academy-id 31799 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162949}} {:db/id 17592186162949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162044 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161838 :question/id #uuid "ba46e82f-10b0-529c-94b0-3aebb7d1e1a6" :question/math-academy-id "e-8678"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e97b8e36-3790-5cdc-bd77-417574af23f3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162719} {:db/id 17592186162720} {:db/id 17592186362258} {:db/id 17592186362259} {:db/id 17592186362260} {:db/id 17592186363189} {:db/id 17592186405174} {:db/id 17592186405181}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ab944e55-c021-5455-a8c9-8144173eabb7" :step/math-academy-id 32221 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162900}}] :activity/title "Reducing a Quadratic Curve to Its Principal Axes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162224} {:db/id 17592186162856 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163231 :tutorial/content "Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables 

$$
\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}
$$

that transforms the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ into the quadratic form $\mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. 

The columns of the matrix $P$ are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of $A,$ which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the **principal axes** of the quadratic form.

Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation 

$$
6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,
$$

and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

![](images/d8/d8a6b6dff52e0c4004432f9447b5fd484612eaacf07588c3469af143b0a9e880.png)

It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,
$$

which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form. 

So, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}6-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +14 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

$\qquad$ $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$

Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes $y_1$ and $y_2.$ 

![](images/10/10a2f0ccd179eba7f65410f932548d954a459e1bc8dcb0803a5b2d9fe7896432.png)

In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to 

$$
7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.
$$

 

Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2} & =14 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{7}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2f9d7d81-cc50-5024-8f69-3b529968aeac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4890 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d3ecee7b-206f-5bb5-9257-61e0758f2151" :step/math-academy-id 30544 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162923}} {:db/id 17592186163231 :tutorial/content "Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. "ec22f795-26e2-5bc9-b423-bed373ca22ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-95809" :question/problem "Find the principal axes of the curve ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=48.$" :question/worked-solution "First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=48
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}+1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=40
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-8.$ 

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)1I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-(-8)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

"Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=2
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$"} :step/id #uuid "c358e7c3-78df-5477-a368-888654cd7c35"} {:db/id 17592186411464 :step/content {:db/id 17592186411460 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24fa485f-91ea-5bd7-b5bf-ff53f7921b30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A  hyperbola with semiaxes  $2$ and $4$" :db/id 17592186411433} {:answer/id #uuid "40462880-f937-54f8-9c63-a892cafb32da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An ellipse with semiaxes  $2$ and $\sqrt{8}$" :db/id 17592186411435} {:answer/id #uuid "69cb5485-7267-5d3c-8e9b-6410002fdbd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola with semiaxes  $\sqrt{8}$ and $4$" :db/id 17592186411438} {:answer/id #uuid "a1267461-8286-578d-8e73-1197cd603858" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A circle with radius  $4$" :db/id 17592186411446} {:answer/id #uuid "efcf49e3-8778-553a-9158-db5800030dbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "Two parallel lines" :db/id 17592186411453}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411433} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fdaee3e-396b-5d40-981f-615ed5526c05" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411455}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6abf962b-d107-56b7-9263-80678639c14a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95002" :question/problem "Which curve is defined by the equation $3{x}_{1}^{2}+10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}=32?$" :question/worked-solution "Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.  

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 5 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & 5 \\ 5 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda -16 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =8,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $8{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2} & =32 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes  $2$ and $4.$"} :step/id #uuid "226f8cb7-5c22-5a4b-8d5c-99f40fa38b6f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186411466}} {:db/id 17592186411466 :step/content {:db/id 17592186411461 $$

$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=40
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-8.$ 

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)1I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-(-8)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, to calculate the inverse of a quadratic function, we must first restrict its domain.

As an example, let's consider the following quadratic function:

$$
f(x)=(x-2)^2-3
$$

 

Since the function is in vertex form, we can immediately see that the vertex of the corresponding parabola $y=f(x)$ is located at $(2,-3).$ Therefore, the function $f(x)$ will be one-to-one if we restrict its domain to either $x\leq 2$ or $x\geq 2.$ 

Let's restrict the domain to $x\geq 2.$ The graph of $y=f(x)$ for $x\geq 2$ is shown below.

![](images/05/059fc0ffddc4b590de8597d3252a6901c7da16063e16b2b4a9a7b24383ce83f7.png)

Now that $f(x)$ is one-to-one, we can calculate its inverse. We follow the four usual steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y.$

$$
y = (x-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y.$

$$
x = (y-2)^2 - 3
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(y-2)^{2}-3 \\ x+3 & =(y-2)^{2} \\ \sqrt{x+3} & =y-2 \\ \sqrt{x+3}+2 & =y\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** The *domain* of the original function is the *range* of the inverse function. In our case, since the domain of $f$ is $x \geq 2,$ the range of the inverse must be $f^{-1} \geq 2.$ Therefore, we select the positive square root in the third step above. Indeed, notice that $\sqrt{x + 3} +2 \geq 2.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x).$

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x + 3} +2
$$

We're done!" :tutorial/id #uuid "783dd423-f37c-5794-a3be-b018f146724c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9258 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c88a3ac6-6ff0-5d00-811e-a83529593d3d" Consider the vector field $F=-3\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=-3\,j$ is parallel to ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through ${C}_{2}$ will cancel with the net outflow through ${C}_{4}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.

:topic/math-academy-id 3715} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180343 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180789 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

By drawing an outward-pointing unit normal vector, it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$

When measuring flux through a closed curve, the curve's orientation does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same in either case. 

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is also positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "36b855d8-9994-5c22-bbc4-e28065875f84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9523 :tutorial/title "Orientation-Independence"} :step/id #uuid "a000a04f-fdd8-5b25-9b23-e59a14a3592d" :step/math-academy-id 184957 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180344}} {:db/id 17592186180344 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179644 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179482 :question/id #uuid "c427d9b4-2944-5edc-8e19-363de348d23d" :question/math-academy-id "e-15147"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b7b8782-d1f4-5654-a18f-6ad35de8fb30" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049212} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186050104}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180031} {:db/id 17592186180032} {:db/id 17592186262687} {:db/id 17592186262688} {:db/id 17592186262690} {:db/id 17592186262691} {:db/id 17592186420910} {:db/id 17592186420911} {:db/id 17592186420912} {:db/id 17592186420914}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining a Flux's Sign From a Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "4f8760a0-8c8e-5ec6-9492-0ecc32789da6" :step/math-academy-id 184958 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180345}} {:db/id 17592186180345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180346 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179645 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179483 :question/id #uuid "15426c37-1508-5407-ab49-b26f8761795c" :question/math-academy-id "e-15148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9c8ca56-5ea8-547c-80ab-6b1f1347447e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180034} {:db/id 17592186180035} {:db/id 17592186235531} {:db/id 17592186262697} {:db/id 17592186262698} {:db/id 17592186262699} {:db/id 17592186262700} {:db/id 17592186262701} {:db/id 17592186362496} {:db/id 17592186420909} {:db/id 17592186420913}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for Flux"} :step/id #uuid "2c288a88-997c-5ef1-98ff-24092e7506f9" :step/math-academy-id 184962 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180347}} {:db/id 17592186180347 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid ![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid "5c82115b-5b07-5765-b4a2-64382478cffb" :step/math-academy-id 184965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180348}} {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. unit step function." :question/worked-solution "The second shifting theorem states that if $a \ge 0$ and $\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\}$ exists for $s > s_0,$ then

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\}
= e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+a)\big\},
\qquad \text{for} \; s > s_0,
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ u(t-2)\big(t^2+3t+2\big) \right\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=2,$ and we have 

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-2)\,g(t)\big\} = e^{-2s}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+2)\big\},
$$

where $g(t)=t^2+3t+2.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+2) & =(t+2)^{2}+3(t+2)+2 \\  & ={t}^{2}+4t+4\,+\,3t+6\,+\,2 \\  & ={t}^{2}+7t+12.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathcal{L} \big\{t^n\big\}=\dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ and $\mathcal{L} \{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+2)} & =L{{t}^{2}+7t+12} \\  & =L{{t}^{2}}+7L{t}+12L{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+7\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+12\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{7}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{12}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-2s}\,L{g(t+2)} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{7}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{12}{s}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049877} {:db/id 17592186050458} {:db/id 17592186221928 :question/id #uuid "07fc3c3a-eefd-5543-8284-0927f58d76cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-326384" :knowledge-point/_questions $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+4)} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(9\pi t)} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+81{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
L{u(t-2)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)}.
$$

$$
L{u(t-2)\,g(t)}={e}^{-2s}\,L{g(t+2)},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+2) & =sin\,(\pi (t+2)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t+2\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+2)} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-2s}\,L{g(t+2)} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\big\} = e^{-as}F(s),
$$

where $F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}.$

In our case, we wish to find the transform of

$$
u(t-1)(t-1)^3.
$$

 

By comparing this expression to the form in the theorem, we can identify the following:

- The shift is $a = 1.$

- The shifted function is $f(t-1) = (t-1)^3.$

From the shifted function, we can deduce the original unshifted function $f(t)$ by simply replacing $(t-1)$ with $t{:}$

$$
f(t) = t^3.
$$

Now, we calculate the Laplace transform $F(s)$ of the unshifted function using the rule $\mathcal{L}\{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}{:}$

$$
F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{t^3\} = \dfrac{3!}{s^{3+1}} = \dfrac{6}{s^4}.
$$

Finally, we apply the shifting theorem formula $\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\big\} = e^{-as}F(s)$ by multiplying $F(s)$ by the exponential delay factor $e^{-s}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-1)(t-1)^{3}} & ={e}^{-s}\cdot F(s) \\  & ={e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186222033 :question/id #uuid "d616ff98-be75-57e2-bce9-5627795650c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-342318"} {:db/id 17592186222034 :question/id #uuid $$

$$

In our case, we wish to find the transform of

$$
u(t-6)(t-6)^{2}.
$$

By comparing this expression to the form in the theorem, we can identify the following:

- The shift is $a=6.$

- The shifted function is $f(t-6)=(t-6)^{2}.$

From the shifted function, we can deduce the original unshifted function $f(t)$ by simply replacing $(t-6)$ with $t:$

$$
f(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

$$

17592186222370 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222526 :tutorial/content "The **unit step function** $u(t-a)$ acts like a switch:

- If $t < a$, then $u(t-a)=0$.

- If $t \ge a$, then $u(t-a)=1$.

So, when we multiply a function $g(t)$ by $u(t-a)$, the function becomes

$$
{\begin{aligned}0, & t<a, \\ g(t), & t\ge a.\end{aligned}
$$

This operation "switches on" the function $g(t)$ at time $t=a$.

For example, consider the function $y(t)=u(t-2) \cdot \dfrac14 t^2.$ Here, $a=2$ and $g(t) = \dfrac{1}{4}t^2,$ so

$$
{\begin{aligned}0, & t<2, \\ \frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}, & t\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

The plot of this function is shown below. Note that the curve follows the parabola for $t \ge 2$ but is zero for $t < 2$.

![](images/04/04398ba96ee11b0f99405b6890ec2c16070460e45bbe7aec1630ec27698d0b93.png)

Suppose we know the Laplace transform of $g(t).$ We'll now learn how to find the Laplace transform of $u(t-a)\,g(t).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4a22f9b9-23e6-503b-9c4d-1b5a100a6aa5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14741 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "76a7d3b3-6b52-5a8e-bdef-581b35cb59f7" :step/math-academy-id 600720 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222371}} {:db/id 17592186222371 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222477 :tutorial/content "From the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}
=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}u(t-a)g(t)\,\textrm{d}t.
$$

Because $u(t-a)=0$ for $t < a$ and $u(t-a)=1$ for $t\ge a$, the integrand is zero until $t=a$.
So the integral reduces to

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}
=\int_a^\infty e^{-st}g(t)\,\textrm{d}t.
$$

To compare this with a standard Laplace transform, we shift the variable of integration so that the lower limit is $0$.

Let $\tau=t-a$. Then $t=\tau+a$ and $\textrm{d}t=\textrm{d}\tau$. Also, when $t=a$, we have $\tau=0$.

Substituting gives

$$
\int_a^\infty e^{-st}g(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=\int_0^\infty e^{-s(\tau+a)}g(\tau+a)\,\textrm{d}\tau.
$$

Now separate the exponential term:

$$
e^{-s(\tau+a)}=e^{-as}e^{-s\tau}.
$$

This allows us to factor out the constant $e^{-as}$:

$$
\int_0^\infty e^{-s(\tau+a)}g(\tau+a)\,\textrm{d}\tau
=e^{-as}\int_0^\infty e^{-s\tau}g(\tau+a)\,\textrm{d}\tau.
$$

The remaining integral has exactly the form of a Laplace transform, so recognize

$$
\int_0^\infty e^{-s\tau}g(\tau+a)\,\textrm{d}\tau
=\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\}.
$$

Putting everything together, we obtain the **second shifting theorem**:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}
=e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\},
\qquad \text{for } s>s_0
$$

The key takeaway is that the unit step shifts the *start time* of the function to $t=a$, and changing variables shifts it back to $0$. The exponential factor $e^{-as}$ records this delay in the $s$-domain." :tutorial/id #uuid "78179940-a5e4-5e62-a269-1f11e9e978bf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14334 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Second 17592186222374 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222524 :tutorial/content "We begin with the second shifting theorem:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a) g(t)\}
= e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\}.
$$

In many applications, the function multiplied by the unit step already appears in the shifted form

$$
u(t-a)\,f(t-a).
$$

Our goal is to rewrite the theorem so that this structure can be handled directly.

Suppose $f(t)$ is a function with Laplace transform

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s).
$$

To match the form $u(t-a)f(t-a)$, define

$$
g(t)=f(t-a).
$$

Then the left-hand side becomes

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a) g(t)\}
=\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\}.
$$

Next, determine what happens to the right-hand side.
If $g(t)=f(t-a)$, then

$$
g(t+a)=f\big((t+a)-a\big)=f(t).
$$

So,

$$
\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\}=\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s).
$$

Substituting these results into the theorem gives

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\}
= e^{-as}F(s).
$$

This is the **alternative form of the second shifting theorem**.

Next, we will apply this formula to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4b75df16-a3fb-58a6-80a7-1bd34712e16e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14716 :tutorial/title "Alternative Form of the Second Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "39287031-f3bc-53dd-a472-3a996c44f0d7" :step/math-academy-id 600728 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222375}} {:db/id 17592186222375 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221442 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221205 :question/id #uuid "1b27851d-3630-506e-972c-b6cef8dbeae3" :question/math-academy-id "e-21864"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d22ba3ca-cf7a-5a77-abf6-8620076552bb" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222033} {:db/id 17592186222034} {:db/id 17592186317300} {:db/id 17592186317302} {:db/id 17592186317303} {:db/id 17592186317304} {:db/id 17592186372811}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Alternative Form of the Second Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "1f6fcaea-7f50-52de-86e2-2be948ab6086" :step/math-academy-id 600729}] :activity/title "The Second Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221463} {:db/id 17592186222370 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222526 :tutorial/content "The **unit step function** $u(t-a)$ acts like a switch:

= e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\}.
$$

In many applications, the function multiplied by the unit step already appears in the shifted form

$$
u(t-a)\,f(t-a).
$$

Our goal is to rewrite the theorem so that this structure can be handled directly.

Suppose $f(t)$ is a function with Laplace transform

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s).
$$

To match the form $u(t-a)f(t-a)$, define

$$
g(t)=f(t-a).
$$

Then the left-hand side becomes

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a) g(t)\}
=\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\}.
$$

Next, determine what happens to the right-hand side.
If $g(t)=f(t-a)$, then

$$
g(t+a)=f\big((t+a)-a\big)=f(t).
$$

So,

$$
\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\}=\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s).
$$

Substituting these results into the theorem gives

$$
\mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\,f(t-a)\}
= e^{-as}F(s).
$$

This is the **alternative form of the second shifting theorem**.
