want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{0}^{1}\int_{x}^{2x} (x-2y) \ \mathrm{d}  y \ \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

Notice that the domain of integration is a type I region. 

To compute this integral, we must bear the following important points in mind.

- We start with the inner integral, as usual.

- When integrating with respect to $y,$ we treat $x$ as though it were a constant.

- The limits of integration for the inner integral are functions of $x.$ Once again, we treat $x$ as though it were a constant and substitute the integration limits as usual. After this step, there should be no more $y$'s in our integral.

- Finally, we compute the outer integral.

Let's apply these steps to solve the given problem.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{2x}(x-2y)\text{ }dy]\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[xy-{y}^{2}]_{x}^{2x}\text{ }dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x\cdot (2x)-{(2x)}^{2}]-[x\cdot (x)-(x)^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[2{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}]-[{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx & =-2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{[{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[{1}^{3}-{0}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3698e7e3-4bc2-5db0-96b5-172131284b4a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4262 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Repeated Integrals With Variable Limits"} :step/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186135083 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{0}^{1}\int_{x}^{2x} (x-2y) \ \mathrm{d}  y \ \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

Notice that the domain of integration is a type I region. 

To compute this integral, we must bear the following important points in mind.

- We start with the inner integral, as usual.

- When integrating with respect to $y,$ we treat $x$ as though it were a constant.

- The limits of integration for the inner integral are functions of $x.$ Once again, we treat $x$ as though it were a constant and substitute the integration limits as usual. After this step, there should be no more $y$'s in our integral.

- Finally, we compute the outer integral.

Let's apply these steps to solve the given problem.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{2x}(x-2y)\text{ }dy]\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[xy-{y}^{2}]_{x}^{2x}\text{ }dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x\cdot (2x)-{(2x)}^{2}]-[x\cdot (x)-(x)^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[2{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}]-[{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx & =-2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{[{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[{1}^{3}-{0}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3698e7e3-4bc2-5db0-96b5-172131284b4a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4262 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Repeated Integrals With Variable Limits"} :step/id #uuid "59bc86e8-4dae-564b-ab2b-c8ac5309d3be" :step/math-academy-id 25908 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134757}} {:db/id 17592186135083 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to evaluate the repeated integral

}_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{x}^{1/x}y\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{x}^{1/x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}}-x]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{3}+1-(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{11}{6}) \\  & =\frac{11}{12}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "098028bf-3706-5127-9bb7-debd78e7b253" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408136}} {:db/id 17592186408134 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408132 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "100fac5f-cc12-56dc-9567-ee01010ba781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186408119} {:answer/id #uuid "1377aca7-a017-58fe-8e23-256c042e11b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186408120} {:answer/id #uuid "3aabdbf2-aad9-5028-8b69-34e437771408" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14}{15}" :db/id 17592186408121} {:answer/id #uuid "41ea5617-4c16-5bdc-a231-c9432f86dc81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{18}" :db/id 17592186408122} {:answer/id #uuid "93d7f804-0816-5794-84e7-a2fe566f8c71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{5}" :db/id 17592186408127}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186408121} :answer-field/id #uuid "85ef2574-1c06-549a-a456-4b22b82491c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408130}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ffe5914e-4912-5ff3-9b15-3a1462960003" :question/math-academy-id "q-132285" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy\,dx=$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}]_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-{x}^{4}-{x}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{4})\,dx & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+1-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{14}{15}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "20fb188a-faf6-5a84-b51f-1b3b2dd89239"} {:db/id 17592186408135 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351296 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a7ddc79-cbfd-59b5-9638-d178b71104a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e" :db/id 17592186348536} {:answer/id #uuid "4b79160f-37ab-5192-8514-437d9b279188" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186349138} {:answer/id #uuid "544819eb-b6d1-5a40-bb3a-d34d78eef696" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{2}" :db/id 17592186349218} {:answer/id #uuid "a06fce6a-f06f-595a-9863-76102c8d8305" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186349871} {:answer/id #uuid "f06aa1a1-4329-543e-8ec1-01bf70f9f867" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186350550}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349871} :answer-field/id #uuid "08077c01-ccff-5e05-a424-ef1243bb7696" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350720}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b8f9d362-d296-527d-b3eb-8711496d6537" :question/math-academy-id "q-81367" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines
$x=e,$ $y=e$ and the curve $y={e}^{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/aa/aa635ca5ef3198fea56d684b034de476a72e4ace2a4c51b37c6c59977036eb76.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=e$ intercepts the curve $y={e}^{x}$ at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$1\le x\le e.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/b7/b78021a06c9fea100b75c66a619c425345cda3666d84da018895be15a53af06d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,e\le y\le {e}^{x}\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{y\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)]}_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "597be508-6945-5d32-9627-435849b9418f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408134}} {:db/id 17592186408136 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323953 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b726bfa-ba4c-5d91-9f6d-6a3764d8755d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)" :db/id 17592186321242} {:answer/id #uuid "1594e17d-7011-5f7d-aa6a-12336ec25a8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186321322} {:answer/id #uuid "2b5f94c5-0d1b-5f79-944c-8cb9d821beed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)" :db/id 17592186321479} {:answer/id #uuid "564621d9-f224-5fff-b159-cf3615e51a9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186321828} {:answer/id #uuid "d4f698ad-bda0-5b89-8175-c64721d84bac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186322805}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321479} :answer-field/id #uuid "9eb45d35-7041-5bf4-8524-44adec58ddbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323477}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ad4a8e76-c297-5cff-8131-747df131b332" :question/math-academy-id "q-37865" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA,$

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{-x+1}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{1}{1+x+y}]}_{0}^{-x+1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{1+x+(1-x)}-(-\frac{1}{1+x+0}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx\end{aligned}

$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x[\,y\,]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[y]_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b1d9c3ed-33de-5684-8d99-d7f5f9b0c7e9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482657}} {:db/id 17592186482654 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351293 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "357e7017-c759-53cd-bd18-3b9cac8a059e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx" :db/id 17592186348931} {:answer/id #uuid "7bb83aea-26c4-5042-8913-2833d34004fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{2}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx" :db/id 17592186349582} {:answer/id #uuid "89dc3879-a9e4-5291-a430-52520db7f2af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{2}[{\int }_{3-{x}^{2}}^{x+1}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx" :db/id 17592186349697} {:answer/id #uuid "e3f30da7-1720-596a-b960-80e3393eccfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx" :db/id 17592186350448} {:answer/id #uuid "f54b2107-78b3-5b8f-b15e-e4e04bce393b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{3-{x}^{2}}^{x+1}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx" :db/id 17592186350592}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350448} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e294541-5f38-5092-8793-4eff75d982fb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350763}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a289df3d-5c34-5bee-85db-98d71fbc43da" :question/math-academy-id "q-81340" :question/problem "If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=3-{x}^{2}$ and $y=x+1,$ then ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/73/7316d667d7308ac5ec0f5348055d3d0e7eb90b97abaa74f5693c3151dc3b8bb1.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{x}^{2} & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/aa/aab6fb99694b518bfa9d200a75876c9e888ba1ab7d699464bc9caca360be775a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x+1\le y\le 3-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e0bceb01-13f0-500a-a70e-d7c56dc36189" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482656}} {:db/id 17592186482656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351295 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6ba8975f-1dcf-5982-82b5-4619f25392af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186349440} {:answer/id #uuid "909c8869-f444-52b1-8e81-f3f7d8cd7ea7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186349746} {:answer/id #uuid "9cd6c44c-c13b-51de-a23a-1e56014ae0e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81}{2}" :db/id 17592186349844} {:answer/id #uuid "a3dbc989-fd06-546f-a58e-5a71b4609f5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "19" :db/id 17592186349910} {:answer/id #uuid "d230d5cd-76aa-5b60-afae-1d4ccdb5bb52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{41}{2}" :db/id 17592186350291}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349844} :answer-field/id #uuid "cef03a78-3898-53d7-a31f-076237c237e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351068}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bba1a6f7-479e-5c7c-a4a7-2bc8097d537b" :question/math-academy-id "q-81361" :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA,\,$
where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{e}^{y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}-{e}^{0})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x(x-1)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We discard the solution $x=\frac{5}{2}$ since $x\le 0$ in our region. Therefore, $x$-limits are $-2\le x\le 0.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

$$

$$

![](images/73/7316d667d7308ac5ec0f5348055d3d0e7eb90b97abaa74f5693c3151dc3b8bb1.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{x}^{2} & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/aa/aab6fb99694b518bfa9d200a75876c9e888ba1ab7d699464bc9caca360be775a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x+1\le y\le 3-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e0bceb01-13f0-500a-a70e-d7c56dc36189" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482656}} {:db/id 17592186482622 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268853 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a55a9b55-701b-54b8-9dc3-ff767eb9a16b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186267638} {:answer/id #uuid "b89fe4b4-ca5f-5b19-9c79-5f2ac46d2595" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186267800} {:answer/id #uuid "bf6a5ad1-907d-59c7-a9c8-ed050fde1508" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186267859} {:answer/id #uuid "e85875be-4289-5cdd-8c4f-d83917f81081" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186268207} {:answer/id #uuid "fcfb32be-1877-5c91-86e5-ee84568b6b69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186268375}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186268375} :answer-field/id #uuid "9bb0802c-c72d-5b84-a668-8e4527960b23" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268681}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "07938b36-7b86-5365-9a53-980eadb141d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-132276" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx=$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[y]_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/24/24683f81da1c7e90ccbd51748f5f46407137be4a40ef5f0678292b70f0781eff.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2} & =x-1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x+2)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/e9/e955ad94bca70a8e6f996d81814ffa8fcc7a322d5979db7b0726d39558b6aa86.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0ba397eb-27d1-5f99-9aee-673204cdeaff" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483479}} {:db/id 17592186483453 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268855 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "576ddeae-8148-5d98-9276-c4916d082cfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186266923} {:answer/id #uuid "8d3026f4-d919-504f-ae3a-79b5af8301a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}" :db/id 17592186267406} {:answer/id #uuid "c93138df-b030-5c7f-b21f-415d12704304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186267948} {:answer/id #uuid "e2affe66-cebd-58ac-b5cd-9043cda4b543" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186268147} {:answer/id #uuid "ed66d9ac-44b3-55cb-8a98-dbe724a419de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186268251}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267406} :answer-field/id #uuid "eba13f08-f419-5a9a-9957-7c081d134163" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "63aade32-c436-5c43-9ff2-73d45e2de0f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-132282" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,dy\,dx=$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and below the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "Since $y\le 0,$ we obtain

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\,⟹\,y=-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}.
$$

Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/9c/9c6b1dd7d81d124888ddd588027eed908a0eaecb2c42ebc79f3253c4123dbe86.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the circle with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$-1\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/bd/bd584d7481549b792e786a7186ba7ee87cd536258c5a0135f36ee17d96c4880d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\le y\le 0\}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}8x{y}^{3}\,dA={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x[{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}4{y}^{3}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x{[{y}^{4}]}_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x(0-{(-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{2} & =x-1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x+2)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x-1}^{1-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{e}^{y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}-{e}^{0})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x(x-1)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx & ={[{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(64-24)-(1-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =40+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8054baf7-76fc-513c-bc8c-95f9b72f74a0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483480}} {:db/id 17592186483453 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268855 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "576ddeae-8148-5d98-9276-c4916d082cfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186266923} {:answer/id #uuid "8d3026f4-d919-504f-ae3a-79b5af8301a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}" :db/id 17592186267406} {:answer/id #uuid "c93138df-b030-5c7f-b21f-415d12704304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186267948} {:answer/id #uuid "e2affe66-cebd-58ac-b5cd-9043cda4b543" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186268147} {:answer/id #uuid "ed66d9ac-44b3-55cb-8a98-dbe724a419de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}" :db/id 17592186268251}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267406} :answer-field/id #uuid "eba13f08-f419-5a9a-9957-7c081d134163" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "63aade32-c436-5c43-9ff2-73d45e2de0f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-132282" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\frac{4}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,dy\,dx=$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

$$

![](images/9c/9c6b1dd7d81d124888ddd588027eed908a0eaecb2c42ebc79f3253c4123dbe86.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the circle with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$-1\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/bd/bd584d7481549b792e786a7186ba7ee87cd536258c5a0135f36ee17d96c4880d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\le y\le 0\}
$$

$$
{∬}_{D}8x{y}^{3}\,dA={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}8x{y}^{3}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x[{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}4{y}^{3}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x{[{y}^{4}]}_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}^{0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2x(0-{(-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2x(1-{x}^{2})^{2})\,dx & ={[\frac{(1-{x}^{2})^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{(1-{1}^{2})^{3}}{3}-\frac{(1-(-1)^{2})^{3}}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}

$$

"f258f110-e541-5edf-8050-54d03177e499" :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Explicit to the Recursive Formula"}] :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $a_n = 8 \cdot 3^n$ for $n\geq 1$. What is the recursive formula for this sequence?" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_n
$$

To complete the formula, we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1$. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1} &= 8 \cdot 3^{1} = 8 \cdot 3 = 24, \\
a_{2} &= 8 \cdot 3^{2} = 8 \cdot 9 = 72
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
r = \frac{a_{2}}{a_{1}} = \frac{72}{24} = 3
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = 3 a_n, \quad a_1 = 24, \quad n \geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048829} {:db/id 17592186134173 :question/id #uuid "15b1932e-ac02-5bde-8021-8f023502f81f" :question/math-academy-id "q-231496"} {:db/id 17592186134445 :question/id #uuid "f4879140-fbfe-55fb-82e8-9fcf4a805617" :question/math-academy-id "q-44991"} {:db/id 17592186133933 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133536 :question/id #uuid "5537647b-d722-5000-8445-b2743cc1f1f8" :question/math-academy-id "e-1512"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6af17da8-272b-55fb-8a5d-5857bd41051e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050067}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134174 :question/id #uuid "d66dcec1-9266-5a54-878f-9b38ff371348" :question/math-academy-id "q-231658"} {:db/id 17592186134175 :question/id #uuid "09766b8d-78f7-55cd-8e3e-ab7533e74934" :question/math-academy-id "q-231659"}] :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Explicit to the Recursive Formula Using Function Notation"} {:db/id 17592186133536 :question/id #uuid "5537647b-d722-5000-8445-b2743cc1f1f8" :question/math-academy-id "e-1512" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186133933 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6af17da8-272b-55fb-8a5d-5857bd41051e" :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Explicit to the Recursive Formula Using Function Notation"}] :question/problem "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $f(n) =\dfrac{6}{(-2)^n}$ for $n\geq 1$. What is the recursive formula for this sequence?" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = r \cdot f(n)
$$

To complete the formula, we must determine the common ratio $r$ and state the first term $a_1$. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= (6)/((-2)^{1}) = (6)/((-2)) =-3, \\
f(2) &= (6)/((-2)^{2}) = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the common ratio is

$$
r = (f(2))/(f(1)) = ((\frac{3}{2}))/((-3)) =-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula for the geometric sequence is

$$
f(n+1) = -\dfrac{1}{2} f(n), \qquad f(1) = -3, \qquad n \geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050067} {:db/id 17592186134174 :question/id #uuid "d66dcec1-9266-5a54-878f-9b38ff371348" :question/math-academy-id "q-231658"} {:db/id 17592186134175 :question/id #uuid "09766b8d-78f7-55cd-8e3e-ab7533e74934" :question/math-academy-id "q-231659"} {:db/id 17592186133934 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133537 :question/id #uuid "19d183f9-cf05-5477-8da9-642e2fd8e03b" :question/math-academy-id "e-1513"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ac7a8723-02b7-5467-98f7-530ba8239c4f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134176 :question/id #uuid "e8863b9e-f6aa-5a0a-98c3-0faa938a9d5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-231760"} {:db/id 17592186134444 :question/id #uuid "39ed5335-4235-5576-a8bf-bee0d4f106a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-44962"}] :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Recursive to the Explicit Formula"} {:db/id 17592186133537 :question/id #uuid "19d183f9-cf05-5477-8da9-642e2fd8e03b" :question/math-academy-id "e-1513" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186133934 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ac7a8723-02b7-5467-98f7-530ba8239c4f" :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Recursive to the Explicit Formula"}] :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the geometric sequence
$a_{n+1} = 3a_n,\, \qquad a_1 = 1,\, \qquad n\geq 1$?" :question/worked-solution "The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}, \qquad n \geq 1
$$

So, we must determine the first term $a_1$ and the common ratio $r$.

We are given that the first term is $a_1=1$. To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_n
$$

From the above, we see that $r = 3$.

Substituting $a_1 = 1$ and $r = 3$ into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} a_n &= a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot 3^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 3^{n-1}. \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
a_n=3^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134176 :question/id #uuid "e8863b9e-f6aa-5a0a-98c3-0faa938a9d5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-231760"} {:db/id 17592186134444 :question/id #uuid "39ed5335-4235-5576-a8bf-bee0d4f106a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-44962"} {:db/id 17592186133935 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133551 :question/id #uuid "5027a265-fd62-574b-b6fa-2bacf9de7304" :question/math-academy-id "e-4238"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6a910df9-7b4a-5892-a084-52d8b5dcd086" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134179 :question/id #uuid "fa66fa35-d179-5015-a17e-379af36bb042" :question/math-academy-id "q-252358"} {:db/id 17592186134478 :question/id #uuid "a620b69b-cba8-5da5-ad85-4ab981a033c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-51509"}] :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Recursive to the Explicit Formula Using Function Notation"} {:db/id 17592186133551 :question/id #uuid "5027a265-fd62-574b-b6fa-2bacf9de7304" :question/math-academy-id "e-4238" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186133935 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6a910df9-7b4a-5892-a084-52d8b5dcd086" :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Recursive to the Explicit Formula Using Function Notation"}] :question/problem "What is the explicit formula for the $n$th term of the sequence
$f(n+1) =-\dfrac{f(n)}{3},\, \quad f(1) = {\color{blue}9},\, \quad n\geq 1$?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite our recursive formula as follows:

$$
f(n + 1) = - (f(n))/(3) =-\frac{1}{3}f(n)
$$

The explicit formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
f(n) =f(1) \cdot r^{n-1}, \quad n \geq 1
$$

So, we must determine the first term $f(1)$ and the common ratio $r$.

We are given that the first term is

$$
f(1)=9
$$

To find the common ratio, we compare the given sequence with the general recursive formula for a geometric sequence:

$$
f(n+1) = {\color{red}r} \cdot f(n)
$$

From the above, we see that

$$
r = -\dfrac{1}{3}
$$

Substituting

$$
f(1) = 9
$$

and

$$
r = -\dfrac{1}{3}
$$

into the formula for the $n$th term, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} f(n) &= f(1) \cdot r^{n-1} \\[5pt] &= 9 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n-1}. \end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify further by manipulating the exponents as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(n) &= 9 \cdot (-\frac{1}{3})^{n - 1} \\
&= 9 \cdot (-\frac{1}{3})^{-1} \cdot (-\frac{1}{3})^{n} \\
&= 9 \cdot (-\frac{3}{1}) \cdot (-\frac{1}{3})^{n} \\
&=-27 \cdot (1)/((-3)^{n}) \\
&= - (27)/((-3)^{n})
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is

$$
f(n)=-\dfrac{27}{(-3)^n},\quad n\geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134179 :question/id #uuid "fa66fa35-d179-5015-a17e-379af36bb042" :question/math-academy-id "q-252358"} {:db/id 17592186134478 :question/id #uuid "a620b69b-cba8-5da5-ad85-4ab981a033c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-51509"} {:db/id 17592186048166} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186134940} :activity/id #uuid "a09fce56-8cba-5c04-b594-13a87263e94e" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048142 :topic/id #uuid "82d65d50-f769-531a-8e21-07640e0f163f" :topic/math-academy-id 2215} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134940 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135016 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the following **explicit formula** for a geometric sequence:

$$
a_n = 2\cdot 5^n, \qquad n\geq 1
$$

We can write this geometric sequence using a recursive formula. Recall that the recursive formula for *any* geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r\cdot a_n
$$

To convert from the explicit formula to the recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common ratio. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1} &= 2 \cdot 5^{1} = 10 \\
a_{2} &= 2 \cdot 5^{2} = 50
\end{aligned}
$$

and the common ratio is

$$
r = \frac{a_{2}}{a_{1}} = \frac{50}{10} = 5
$$

So, the first term is

$$
a_1={\color{blue}10}
$$

and the common ratio is

$$
r={\color{red}5}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}5} \cdot a_n, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}10}, \qquad n \geq 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cb2e1b6-42f6-5508-aa68-1085dd64e89c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1670 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d53098fa-92a8-5d13-9bb6-afc94451163e" :step/math-academy-id 459983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134941}} {:db/id 17592186134941 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133550 :question/id #uuid "6aa991c4-28e3-51fc-9642-19fa9346202d" :question/math-academy-id "e-4237"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f258f110-e541-5edf-8050-54d03177e499" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048829}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134173} {:db/id 17592186134445}] :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Explicit to the Recursive Formula"} :step/id #uuid "28a0a6a2-8445-5dbf-bab4-94273d8bd5a2" :step/math-academy-id 459984 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134942}} {:db/id 17592186134942 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133933 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133536 :question/id #uuid "5537647b-d722-5000-8445-b2743cc1f1f8" :question/math-academy-id "e-1512"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6af17da8-272b-55fb-8a5d-5857bd41051e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050067}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134174} {:db/id 17592186134175}] :knowledge-point/title "Translating From the Explicit to the Recursive Formula Using Function Notation"} :step/id #uuid "842bc2ad-3287-51df-b12a-9c624c1f5178" :step/math-academy-id 459987 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134943}} {:db/id 17592186134943 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135017 :tutorial/content "It's often more useful to translate from the recursive formula to an explicit one. $$

$$

a_{n + 1} &= r \cdot a_{n} \\

\end{aligned}

Now we substitute

$$
a_1={\color{blue}2}
$$

and

$$

into the formula for the $n$th term:

$$

$$

$$
a_n = 2\cdot 5^n, \qquad n\geq 1
$$

We can write this geometric sequence using a recursive formula. Recall that the recursive formula for *any* geometric sequence is

$$
a_{n+1} = r\cdot a_n
$$

To convert from the explicit formula to the recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common ratio. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1} &= 2 \cdot 5^{1} = 10 \\
a_{2} &= 2 \cdot 5^{2} = 50
\end{aligned}
$$

and the common ratio is

$$
r = \frac{a_{2}}{a_{1}} = \frac{50}{10} = 5
$$

So, the first term is

$$
a_1={\color{blue}10}
$$

and the common ratio is

$$
r={\color{red}5}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}5} \cdot a_n, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}10}, \qquad n \geq 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cb2e1b6-42f6-5508-aa68-1085dd64e89c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1670 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d53098fa-92a8-5d13-9bb6-afc94451163e" :step/math-academy-id 459983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134941}} {:db/id 17592186135016 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the following **explicit formula** for a geometric sequence:

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167262 :question/id #uuid "f3e98464-6e85-513e-a930-d0947c1c72b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-336711" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} ." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$"} {:db/id 17592186396972 :question/id #uuid "68ae00aa-e57d-5620-9c00-ead6febaac73" :question/math-academy-id "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186543471 :question/id #uuid "026f1da3-fe0b-5238-91da-8230388ad940" :question/math-academy-id "q-336702" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{4t}-(-3{e}^{4t})\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -10{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -4{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167186 :question/id #uuid "dc4c9e61-81e1-5e97-95cb-a89bd2a71a0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-330899" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d6e43401-278c-58f1-b818-fad8546bda0e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186303797}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186303797} :answer-field/id #uuid "295a6ea8-2810-531b-90a1-1e521e6ec6e3" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186304170} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "596f4cf7-f992-59e0-a1ab-314f9b22d6b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{e}^{4t}" :db/id 17592186303002} {:answer/id #uuid "5e995f6d-38bc-503f-add8-819490663c94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12e^{4t}" :db/id 17592186496865}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496865} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6a0f445-2c98-5d5e-9321-6d979dc294b5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186304700}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2">$x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}-\,\,\frac{1}{4}$</td>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>

<tr>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">$90t+45$</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=15t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=15\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =15t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 15\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}+\int 15{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}-15{e}^{-t} \\  & =-15{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -15{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}10(1-2t)-60(t+1) \\ 15(1-2t)-60(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}80t+50 \\ 90t+45\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186515600 :question/id #uuid "ca58d00f-a386-5b1e-a85b-e37b24ea3447" :question/math-academy-id "q-337284" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33978283-6287-570d-93ab-bb7631c431be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3t-1" :db/id 17592186514988}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186514988} :answer-field/id #uuid "d5413a60-3a3a-5440-92ee-5f361e71fff8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186515496}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3t-1 \\ 3(t-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "112cd61c-d6ec-5b21-a43e-abee24d650f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "integrating" :db/id "41fc66cd-f988-5c35-8b92-ae13cc6708fa" :topic/math-academy-id 3187} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167991 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.

In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\,u(t))^{′} \\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\Phi^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99630576-f78f-593a-af83-87c98421e2c0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14396 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "94760db8-7585-5363-8838-c0f44735b806" $$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

$$

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & -6{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{t} \\ 6{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-6{e}^{2t})-5{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{2t} & -5{e}^{2t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{2t} & -5{e}^{2t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{3t} & -5{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-2t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{3t} & -5{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-2t} & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{t} \\ 6{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}12{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 12{e}^{4t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{4t} \\ -{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & -6{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{4t} \\ -{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5{e}^{t} \\ 9{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "263c0b72-c299-51ac-98e0-f88dd4d823d3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497452}} {:db/id 17592186497449 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167175 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08055b09-dc8e-5e64-a169-6b8646c97e18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-18t-15" :db/id 17592186302508}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186302508} :answer-field/id #uuid "6e093a4e-16c7-597e-9369-a2860151d355" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186304378}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a6dc5997-1d4e-5312-9245-798d648973c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-329817" :question/problem "$$

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 8t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t} \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=8t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=8\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =8t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 8\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}+\int 8\,{e}^{-t}\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}-8{e}^{2t} \\  & =-8{e}^{-t}(1+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -8{e}^{-t}(1+t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(1-2t)-16(1+t) \\ 2(1-2t)-8(1+t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-18t-15 \\ -12t-6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7c983da7-ca72-5a73-bf3a-e7f56ec9519d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497428}} {:db/id 17592186497452 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365792 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ff2cccf5-489b-5e70-b3a9-9d2661562299" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186365794} {:answer/id #uuid "4c7d0200-75d6-56dc-9a3b-832b6fae8337" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2e^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186496829}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496829} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef783e3c-2210-5313-90c8-cc217b3c7be3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365793} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "974ddd49-be50-5576-a845-339cab6a2a08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4/3" :db/id 17592186365796} {:answer/id #uuid "0aacdf65-443f-56da-b835-155b66a57197" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186496676}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496676} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4dc56ff-d11b-5257-828e-dfd7f038bf79" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365795}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cab04d20-21da-5031-a5e8-e08eadd456c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336698" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=15t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=15\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =15t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 15\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}+\int 15{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}-15{e}^{-t} \\  & =-15{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -15{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}10(1-2t)-60(t+1) \\ 15(1-2t)-60(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}80t+50 \\ 90t+45\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=15t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=15\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =15t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 15\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}+\int 15{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}-15{e}^{-t} \\  & =-15{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3t-1 \\ 3(t-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0418a620-c5b3-5d53-82c0-63ca1c0bfbbe" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515651}} {:db/id 17592186515624 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311737 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03391546-51e2-592b-b33e-96a0e7dadad4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186308770}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186308770} :answer-field/id #uuid "a4cc6a92-1dbb-533a-bde1-5f5375f2fb88" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311269} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c40bb4a2-ee82-5c62-8098-95674097c15b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186310321}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186310321} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa3b02da-876b-5e0a-8cf7-c53cb24cd812" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311526}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5ea97844-39dd-5c98-b9ff-e503c4be0f51" :question/math-academy-id "q-336699" :question/problem "$$

$$
